activities.title: Why registration is the whole ballgame
activities.question: Why registration is the whole ballgame

cards.title: Eleven activities, one certificate each
cards.law: A unit in IFSC desirous of undertaking any of the listed activities shall obtain a certificate of registration from the Authority (Reg 4(1)).
cards.means: If your activity is on the Reg 4 list, you cannot operate without an IFSCA certificate. If it is not on the list, these regulations do not gate it.
cards.watch: The list is exhaustive. Don't assume a hybrid service is exempt — map it to the nearest listed activity first.
cards.link: Sets up every category playbook in Part 2.

cards.title: Unified registration (since 12 Jan 2026)
cards.law: Proviso to Reg 4(1): a unit undertaking multiple activities may obtain a unified registration, in such manner as may be specified.
cards.means: A multi-desk unit can now hold one unified registration instead of collecting a separate certificate per activity.
cards.watch: Unified registration is NOT unified compliance — each activity still carries its own Chapter IV obligations and its own Part B conduct code.
cards.link: This is the seed of the 'common-or-entity' theme.

cards.title: Company/LLP/body corporate/branch — perpetual
cards.law: Reg 6: a CMI must be present in IFSC as a company, LLP, body corporate, or branch thereof. Reg 13: the certificate is perpetual unless suspended or cancelled.
cards.means: You need a recognised legal vehicle in the IFSC, and once granted, registration does not lapse on a renewal cycle.
cards.watch: 'Perpetual' surprises those used to periodic renewals elsewhere — there is no validity expiry to diarise, only suspension/cancellation risk.
cards.link: Contrast with SEBI-style periodic renewals.

chapters.title: The Net Worth Framework
chapters.description: Category minimums, liquid-net-worth vs balance-sheet, the highest-not-sum rule, and the myth of a deposit.

concepts.title: Net worth: at all times, highest-not-sum, branch
concepts.hook: Multi-category = HIGHEST, never the sum.
concepts.tricky: Instinct says add the minimums. The regulation says take the highest.

concepts.title: Net worth definition & liquid-assets carve-out
concepts.hook: Liquid-assets trio: Broker dealer · Clearing member · Investment banker.
concepts.tricky: Liquid-assets net worth applies to only three categories. Everyone else uses the balance-sheet definition.

activities.title: Net worth: the number inspectors check first
activities.question: Net worth: the number inspectors check first

cards.title: A continuing test, not an entry gate
cards.law: Reg 7(1): an entity shall comply with the net worth requirements in Schedule I, which shall be maintained at all times.
cards.means: Meeting the minimum on application day is not enough; you must stay above it continuously and be able to evidence it.
cards.watch: A quarterly statement of net worth is a mandatory record (Reg 16(1)(d)) — inspectors reconcile it against Schedule I.
cards.link: Ties to Module 5 record-keeping.

cards.title: Three categories measure differently
cards.law: Proviso to Reg 3(1)(cc): for a broker dealer, clearing member or investment banker, 'net worth' means the aggregate value of liquid assets (cash, bank balance, fixed deposits, Government Securities and other specified instruments).
cards.means: These three cannot count illiquid balance-sheet items toward net worth — only liquid assets qualify.
cards.watch: Everyone else uses the ordinary balance-sheet definition. Applying the wrong definition is a common, material error.
cards.link: A signature 'common-or-entity' trap.

cards.title: Multi-category units
cards.law: Reg 7(4): where an entity operates in multiple categories, it shall maintain the highest of the applicable minimum net worth requirements, unless otherwise specified.
cards.means: A unit doing three activities holds the single highest minimum among them — not the sum, not an average.
cards.watch: Do not add the category minimums together; and it is separate from and additional to net worth required for other (non-CMI) activities (Reg 7(3)).
cards.link: Directly tested in the capstone.

cards.title: A continuing test, not an entry gate
cards.law: Reg 7(1): an entity shall comply with the net worth requirements in Schedule I, which shall be maintained at all times.
cards.means: Meeting the minimum on application day is not enough; you must stay above it continuously and be able to evidence it.
cards.watch: A quarterly statement of net worth is a mandatory record (Reg 16(1)(d)) — inspectors reconcile it against Schedule I.
cards.link: Ties to Module 5 record-keeping.

cards.title: Three categories measure differently
cards.law: Proviso to Reg 3(1)(cc): for a broker dealer, clearing member or investment banker, 'net worth' means the aggregate value of liquid assets (cash, bank balance, fixed deposits, Government Securities and other specified instruments).
cards.means: These three cannot count illiquid balance-sheet items toward net worth — only liquid assets qualify.
cards.watch: Everyone else uses the ordinary balance-sheet definition. Applying the wrong definition is a common, material error.
cards.link: A signature 'common-or-entity' trap.

cards.title: Multi-category units
cards.law: Reg 7(4): where an entity operates in multiple categories, it shall maintain the highest of the applicable minimum net worth requirements, unless otherwise specified.
cards.means: A unit doing three activities holds the single highest minimum among them — not the sum, not an average.
cards.watch: Do not add the category minimums together; and it is separate from and additional to net worth required for other (non-CMI) activities (Reg 7(3)).
cards.link: Directly tested in the capstone.

cards.title: A continuous character test
cards.law: Reg 8(1): a CMI shall ensure that the entity and its principal officer, directors/designated partners, key managerial personnel and controlling shareholders are fit and proper persons, at all times.
cards.means: Fairness, integrity, honesty and good reputation — tested not just at entry but continuously, across a defined list of persons.
cards.watch: A disqualifying event (conviction for moral turpitude/economic offence, pending charge sheet, wilful defaulter, fugitive economic offender, etc.) can taint registration mid-life.
cards.link: Feeds change-in-control (Module 5) and enforcement (Module 6).

cards.title: Principal Officer AND a separate Compliance Officer
cards.law: Reg 9(1): a CMI shall designate a principal officer and a separate compliance officer based out of IFSC.
cards.means: These are two distinct designated roles — you cannot collapse them into one person — and both must be located in the IFSC.
cards.watch: 'Separate' and 'based out of IFSC' are both hard requirements; a shared or offshore officer is a defect.
cards.link: Qualification rules attach to both.

cards.title: Education or experience gateway
cards.law: Reg 9(2): the PO and CO must meet specified educational qualifications (professional qualification or PG degree/diploma in finance, law, accountancy, management, commerce, economics, capital market, banking, insurance, actuarial science, fintech, science, technology, engineering or mathematics; or a graduate with five years' financial-services experience; CA/CS/CMA membership qualifies).
cards.means: There is a defined qualification-or-experience gateway; a law graduate is expressly eligible to be Compliance Officer.
cards.watch: The 'graduate + experience' route was amended to five years (from ten) w.e.f. 12 Jan 2026.
cards.link: Amendment-tracking (old-vs-new).

cards.title: A continuous character test
cards.law: Reg 8(1): a CMI shall ensure that the entity and its principal officer, directors/designated partners, key managerial personnel and controlling shareholders are fit and proper persons, at all times.
cards.means: Fairness, integrity, honesty and good reputation — tested not just at entry but continuously, across a defined list of persons.
cards.watch: A disqualifying event (conviction for moral turpitude/economic offence, pending charge sheet, wilful defaulter, fugitive economic offender, etc.) can taint registration mid-life.
cards.link: Feeds change-in-control (Module 5) and enforcement (Module 6).

cards.title: Principal Officer AND a separate Compliance Officer
cards.law: Reg 9(1): a CMI shall designate a principal officer and a separate compliance officer based out of IFSC.
cards.means: These are two distinct designated roles — you cannot collapse them into one person — and both must be located in the IFSC.
cards.watch: 'Separate' and 'based out of IFSC' are both hard requirements; a shared or offshore officer is a defect.
cards.link: Qualification rules attach to both.

cards.title: Reg 15 imports the whole code
cards.law: Reg 15: a CMI shall abide by the Code of Conduct as specified in Schedule II.
cards.means: The code is not optional guidance — it is a binding regulatory obligation for every CMI, enforceable like any other provision.
cards.watch: Schedule II has two parts: Part A binds all CMIs; Part B adds category-specific codes. Don't stop at Part A for a specific desk.
cards.link: Part B surfaces in each category playbook.

cards.title: No manipulation, no false market
cards.law: Part A cl. 4-5: a CMI shall not indulge in manipulative, fraudulent or deceptive transactions/schemes or spread rumours to distort the market, nor create a false market singly or in collusion.

cards.title: Eight years, electronically retrievable
cards.law: Reg 16(1): a CMI shall maintain and preserve specified books, records and documents in electronic retrieval form for a minimum of eight years — including a quarterly statement of net worth and AML/CFT/KYC compliance documentation.
cards.means: A defined record set, kept retrievable for eight years, is mandatory — and it explicitly includes your quarterly net-worth evidence.
cards.watch: 'Electronic retrieval form' and 'eight years' are both hard minimums.
cards.link: Net-worth statement ties back to Module 2.

cards.title: 15 days for officer changes; prior approval for control
cards.law: Reg 17(2): intimate any change in PO, CO or KMP within 15 days. Reg 23: a branch intimates a change in control within 15 days; an IFSC-incorporated CMI needs PRIOR approval of the Authority for a change in control.
cards.means: Different triggers, different clocks — and a branch merely notifies control changes, while an incorporated CMI must seek prior approval.
cards.watch: Confusing 'intimate within 15 days' with 'seek prior approval' is a classic error.
cards.link: A structural common-or-entity nuance (branch vs incorporated).

cards.title: BCP, cyber, risk — and a 30 September audit
cards.law: Reg 20-22: maintain a BCP (annually reviewed), a cyber security/resilience framework, and risk-management/internal controls. Reg 25: an annual compliance audit by a CA/CS/CMA member (or foreign-authorised auditor), furnished to the Authority by 30 September.
cards.means: A resilience stack plus an independent annual compliance audit with a fixed filing date.
cards.watch: The audit report deadline is 30 September of the year — diarise it.
cards.link: Cyber detail sits in the separate CSCRF framework.

recallCards.back: A defined record set, kept retrievable for eight years, is mandatory — and it explicitly includes your quarterly net-worth evidence.

cards.title: Eight years, electronically retrievable
cards.law: Reg 16(1): a CMI shall maintain and preserve specified books, records and documents in electronic retrieval form for a minimum of eight years — including a quarterly statement of net worth and AML/CFT/KYC compliance documentation.
cards.means: A defined record set, kept retrievable for eight years, is mandatory — and it explicitly includes your quarterly net-worth evidence.
cards.watch: 'Electronic retrieval form' and 'eight years' are both hard minimums.
cards.link: Net-worth statement ties back to Module 2.

cards.title: 15 days for officer changes; prior approval for control
cards.law: Reg 17(2): intimate any change in PO, CO or KMP within 15 days. Reg 23: a branch intimates a change in control within 15 days; an IFSC-incorporated CMI needs PRIOR approval of the Authority for a change in control.
cards.means: Different triggers, different clocks — and a branch merely notifies control changes, while an incorporated CMI must seek prior approval.
cards.watch: Confusing 'intimate within 15 days' with 'seek prior approval' is a classic error.
cards.link: A structural common-or-entity nuance (branch vs incorporated).

cards.title: BCP, cyber, risk — and a 30 September audit
cards.law: Reg 20-22: maintain a BCP (annually reviewed), a cyber security/resilience framework, and risk-management/internal controls. Reg 25: an annual compliance audit by a CA/CS/CMA member (or foreign-authorised auditor), furnished to the Authority by 30 September.
cards.means: A resilience stack plus an independent annual compliance audit with a fixed filing date.
cards.watch: The audit report deadline is 30 September of the year — diarise it.
cards.link: Cyber detail sits in the separate CSCRF framework.

recallCards.back: A defined record set, kept retrievable for eight years, is mandatory — and it explicitly includes your quarterly net-worth evidence.

cards.title: Suo motu, usually on notice
cards.law: Reg 37: the Authority may, suo motu or on information/complaint, appoint an inspecting authority to inspect a CMI's books, systems and procedures; notice is given, but may be dispensed with for reasons recorded in writing where investors' interest requires.
cards.means: Inspection can be triggered proactively; you will normally get notice, but not always.
cards.watch: Exchanges/CCs/depositories may separately inspect BD/CM/DP under their bye-laws; joint inspections are possible.
cards.link: BD/CM/DP carry a dual-oversight layer.

cards.title: Suspension or cancellation grounds
cards.law: Reg 41: the Authority may suspend or cancel registration (or take other action) for failures such as breaching conditions, contravening the Act/regulations, furnishing false or misleading information, non-cooperation in inspection, or failing to resolve investor complaints.
cards.means: A defined set of grounds can cost you your registration.
cards.watch: 'Furnishing false or misleading information in any material particular' is its own standalone ground — accuracy to the Authority is not optional.
cards.link: Ties back to information duties (Module 5).

cards.title: Relaxation and the power to be heard
cards.law: Reg 41 action follows process; Reg 44 lets the Authority relax strict enforcement on application with a non-refundable fee, processed within 30 days. Reg 47 repealed the 2021 CMI Regulations.
cards.means: There is a relaxation mechanism, and enforcement is bounded by process; the 2025 regime replaced the 2021 one.
cards.watch: Relaxation is discretionary and fee-bearing — not a right.
cards.link: Historical context: 2021 → 2025.

cards.title: Set by the exchange / clearing corporation
cards.law: Schedule I: broker dealer net worth is 'as specified by the recognised stock exchange'; clearing member net worth is 'as specified by the recognised clearing corporation'.
cards.means: You look to the exchange/CC rulebook for the number, not a fixed USD figure in Schedule I.
cards.watch: But the DEFINITION of net worth for both is liquid assets only (Reg 3(1)(cc) proviso).
cards.link: Liquid-assets test shared with investment bankers.

cards.title: Comply with the MII bye-laws
cards.law: Reg 26: a broker dealer complies with the recognised stock exchange's bye-laws/rules/regulations; a clearing member complies with the recognised clearing corporation's.
cards.means: Your primary operating rulebook is the MII's, layered on top of the CMI Regulations.
cards.watch: This is also why BD/CM face a dual-oversight layer at inspection and enforcement.
cards.link: Module 6 dual oversight.

cards.title: Act across roles without a fresh certificate
cards.law: Reg 5(4)-(5): with the relevant approval, a clearing member may act as a broker dealer, a broker dealer may act as a clearing member, and each may operate across multiple exchanges/CCs — without a separate certificate of registration.
cards.means: Approved role-crossing does not require a new registration, just the MII's approval.
cards.watch: 'Without a separate certificate' is the key phrase — approval, not re-registration.
cards.link: Contrast with adding a genuinely new activity (needs registration).

cards.title: USD 200,000
cards.law: Schedule I, S.No. 3: Credit Rating Agency net worth is USD 200,000 (ordinary balance-sheet definition).
cards.means: A fixed USD figure, measured on the standard net-worth definition (not liquid assets).
cards.watch: Don't apply the liquid-assets carve-out here — that's only BD/CM/IB.
cards.link: Contrast with Module 7.

cards.title: Written agreement per client
cards.law: Reg 28(1): a CRA shall enter into a written agreement with each client whose securities it proposes to rate, setting out rights, liabilities and fees.
cards.means: Every rating relationship is documented up front, including the fee.
cards.watch: No agreement, no rating — the agreement is the foundation.
cards.link: Ties to conflict-management duties in Part B.

cards.title: Continuous monitoring; constrained withdrawal
cards.law: Reg 28(4)-(5): a CRA shall continuously monitor and periodically review ratings unless withdrawn, and shall generally not withdraw a rating while the rated obligations remain outstanding (subject to specified exceptions).
cards.means: A rating is a living obligation — monitored over its life, not a one-off opinion.
cards.watch: Withdrawal while obligations are outstanding is the exception, not the norm.
cards.link: Enforcement exposure if monitoring lapses.

cards.title: Custody separated from everything else
cards.law: Reg 29(1): a custodian shall separate and segregate its custodian activities from all other activities.
cards.means: Custody is ring-fenced operationally from the entity's other business lines.
cards.watch: Commingling custody with other activities is the cardinal custodian sin.
cards.link: Reinforced by Part B custodian conduct.

cards.title: Client agreement + anti-manipulation controls
cards.law: Reg 29(3)-(4): a custodian enters an agreement with each client detailing custody circumstances, and maintains adequate internal controls to prevent manipulation of records and to protect them from theft and natural hazard.
cards.means: Documented client terms plus hard controls over the integrity and safety of records.
cards.watch: Records protection covers both manipulation and physical loss.
cards.link: Ties to eight-year record-keeping (Module 5).

cards.title: USD 1.5 million — the highest fixed figure

cards.means: The largest fixed Schedule I minimum, reflecting the trustee's fiduciary weight.
cards.watch: Higher than the custodian's USD 1 million.
cards.link: Highest-of rule tests (Module 2).

cards.title: No conflict; agreement before subscription
cards.law: Reg 30(1)-(2): a DT enters an agreement with the issuer before the subscription list opens, and shall not be appointed where it is an associate of the issuer or is likely to have a conflict of interest.
cards.means: Independence from the issuer is a precondition, locked in before the issue opens.
cards.watch: Associate status or likely conflict is disqualifying.
cards.link: Conflict duties echo Part A.

cards.title: Reporting cadence and nominee director on default
cards.law: Reg 30(3): the DT calls for periodic reports within seven days of the relevant board meeting or within forty-five days of the quarter, whichever is earlier; and appoints a nominee director on the issuer's board on two consecutive interest defaults, or default in security creation, or default in redemption.
cards.means: A defined reporting clock and an automatic escalation lever protecting holders.
cards.watch: 'Two consecutive defaults' in interest is the specific nominee-director trigger.
cards.link: A precise number worth memorising.

cards.title: Set by the depository
cards.law: Schedule I, S.No. 6: Depository Participant net worth is 'as specified by the depository'.
cards.means: Look to the recognised depository for the figure, not a fixed Schedule I number.
cards.watch: Like BD/CM, the number lives in the MII rulebook — but the DP uses the ordinary net-worth definition, not liquid assets.
cards.link: Contrast with BD/CM liquid-assets test.

cards.title: Separate accounts per beneficial owner
cards.law: Reg 31(2): a DP shall open separate accounts in the name of each beneficial owner and segregate each owner's securities — never mixed with other owners' or the participant's own securities.
cards.means: Every beneficial owner's holdings are individually accounted and never commingled.
cards.watch: Mixing client holdings with proprietary holdings is a core breach.
cards.link: Echoes custodian segregation.

cards.title: Daily reconciliation with the depository
cards.law: Reg 31(5): a DP shall reconcile its records with the depository on a daily basis; and, where records are electronic, maintain data-processing integrity at all times (31(4)).
cards.means: Reconciliation is a daily obligation, not periodic.
cards.watch: 'Daily' is the operative cadence — a weekly or monthly cycle is non-compliant.
cards.link: Ties to record-keeping and controls.

cards.title: USD 50,000
cards.law: Schedule I, S.No. 7: Distributor net worth is USD 50,000 (ordinary definition).
cards.means: A low fixed floor, on the standard net-worth basis.
cards.watch: Low capital, high conduct scrutiny — the risk here is conduct, not capital.
cards.link: Part B conduct is the real weight.

cards.title: Defined distribution permissions
cards.law: Reg 32(1): a distributor may distribute capital market products/services to clients in IFSC or foreign jurisdictions (from regulated entities in India/IFSC/specified jurisdictions), to sophisticated investors more broadly, and to clients in India from IFSC/specified-jurisdiction providers.
cards.means: Who you may distribute to depends on the client type and the provider's jurisdiction.
cards.watch: The permission set is specific — sophisticated-investor distribution is wider than retail.
cards.link: Client classification drives scope.

cards.title: No mis-selling, no rebates
cards.law: Schedule II Part B (distributor): avoid mis-selling; act in clients' best interests; disclose material information; abstain from attracting clients through rebate; segregate proprietary investments; ensure advertisements are accurate, true, fair and complete.
cards.means: A dense anti-mis-selling, anti-inducement conduct code sits on top of Part A.
cards.watch: Offering rebates to attract clients is expressly prohibited.
cards.link: Contrast with IA fiduciary/no-third-party-fee duties.

cards.title: USD 25,000

cards.means: A low fixed floor, matching the adviser/research-entity tier.

cards.title: A disclosure-led conduct model
cards.law: Reg 33(3)-(4): an ERDPP shall adhere to its code of conduct on a 'comply or explain' basis and disclose its compliance with that code.
cards.means: Rather than rigid rules, the ERDPP either complies or publicly explains departures.
cards.watch: 'Comply or explain' is distinctive — this is not the CRA's prescriptive rating regime.

cards.title: ESG products, not credit ratings
cards.law: The ERDPP deals in ESG ratings and data products, a separate category from credit rating agencies.
cards.means: Don't map CRA duties onto an ERDPP — they are different registrations with different codes.
cards.watch: Treating an ERDPP like a CRA is a category error.
cards.link: Capstone common-or-entity trap.

concepts.title: IA: fiduciary, fee-only, 15-day own-account

activities.title: Investment advisers: fiduciary, fee-only, conflict-clean

cards.title: Act in the client's interest, disclose conflicts
cards.law: Reg 34(3): an investment adviser shall act in a fiduciary capacity towards its clients and disclose all conflicts of interest as and when they arise.
cards.means: The adviser is legally bound to put the client first and surface conflicts continuously.
cards.watch: Fiduciary is a higher bar than mere fair dealing.
cards.link: Contrast with distributor's suitability duties.

cards.title: No consideration from anyone but the client
cards.law: Reg 34(4): an IA shall not receive remuneration or compensation in any form from any person other than the client being advised, in respect of the underlying products.
cards.means: No product commissions or third-party payments — the adviser is paid only by the advised client.
cards.watch: This is the sharpest line between an adviser and a distributor.
cards.link: Distributor can be product-remunerated; adviser cannot.

cards.title: 15-day own-account restriction
cards.law: Reg 34(6): an IA shall not transact on its own account contrary to advice given to clients for 15 days from the advice (with a 24-hour-notice exception if its assessment genuinely changes).
cards.means: The adviser cannot trade against its own live advice within the window.
cards.watch: The exception requires a revised assessment communicated to the client at least 24 hours in advance.
cards.link: A precise, testable rule.

activities.title: Investment bankers: issue management, liquid-assets net worth
activities.question: Investment bankers: issue management, liquid-assets net worth

cards.title: USD 100,000 — liquid assets
cards.law: Schedule I, S.No. 10: Investment Banker net worth is USD 100,000; and per Reg 3(1)(cc), net worth for an investment banker means liquid assets.
cards.means: A fixed USD 100,000 floor, but measured only on liquid assets.
cards.watch: The liquid-assets test is shared with broker dealers and clearing members.
cards.link: Module 7 liquid-assets trio.

cards.title: Agreement with the issuer; demarcated leads
cards.law: Reg 35(1)-(2): an IB enters an agreement with the issuer specifying its roles and responsibilities; where there are multiple lead investment bankers, each one's responsibilities are clearly demarcated.
cards.means: The engagement is documented, and in a syndicate each lead's remit is delineated.
cards.watch: Undemarcated lead responsibilities are a governance gap.
cards.link: Ties to conduct Part B for IBs.

cards.title: Promoter/associate → marketing only
cards.law: Reg 35(3): where the IB is a promoter or associate of the issuer (or of a person making an offer), it shall not undertake any activity except marketing of the issue/offer.
cards.means: Closeness to the issuer collapses the IB's permissible role down to marketing.
cards.watch: This is a bright-line conflict limit, not a disclosure-only duty.
cards.link: Contrast with CRA/adviser conflict-management.

recallCards.back: A fixed USD 100,000 floor, but measured only on liquid assets.

cards.title: USD 100,000 — liquid assets
cards.law: Schedule I, S.No. 10: Investment Banker net worth is USD 100,000; and per Reg 3(1)(cc), net worth for an investment banker means liquid assets.
cards.means: A fixed USD 100,000 floor, but measured only on liquid assets.
cards.watch: The liquid-assets test is shared with broker dealers and clearing members.
cards.link: Module 7 liquid-assets trio.

cards.title: Agreement with the issuer; demarcated leads
cards.law: Reg 35(1)-(2): an IB enters an agreement with the issuer specifying its roles and responsibilities; where there are multiple lead investment bankers, each one's responsibilities are clearly demarcated.
cards.means: The engagement is documented, and in a syndicate each lead's remit is delineated.
cards.watch: Undemarcated lead responsibilities are a governance gap.
cards.link: Ties to conduct Part B for IBs.

cards.title: Promoter/associate → marketing only
cards.law: Reg 35(3): where the IB is a promoter or associate of the issuer (or of a person making an offer), it shall not undertake any activity except marketing of the issue/offer.
cards.means: Closeness to the issuer collapses the IB's permissible role down to marketing.
cards.watch: This is a bright-line conflict limit, not a disclosure-only duty.
cards.link: Contrast with CRA/adviser conflict-management.

recallCards.back: A fixed USD 100,000 floor, but measured only on liquid assets.

chapters.title: Research Entities
chapters.description: Independence, analyst trading control, and the registration exemption.

activities.title: Research entities: independence, and the registration exemption
activities.question: Research entities: independence, and the registration exemption

cards.title: No separate registration if already IA/CRA/FME
cards.law: Reg 4(4): a person need not obtain separate registration as a 'Research Entity' if it is an investment adviser or credit rating agency or Fund Management Entity registered with the Authority that issues, circulates or distributes research reports to the public.
cards.means: Existing registrants issuing public research aren't forced into a second registration.
cards.watch: The exemption is specific to IA/CRA/FME registrants — not a blanket exemption.
cards.link: Registration mapping (Module 1).

cards.title: Ring-fence research from other business
cards.law: Reg 36(4): a research entity shall have appropriate mechanisms to ensure the independence of its research activities from its other business activities.
cards.means: Research must be insulated from the pressures of the entity's other lines.
cards.watch: Independence is structural, not merely aspirational.
cards.link: Echoes IB/adviser conflict controls.

cards.title: Control analyst dealing
cards.law: Reg 36(1),(5)-(6): written policies governing employee/analyst dealing and trading; personal trading of analysts monitored, recorded and, where necessary, subject to formal approval.
cards.means: Analyst personal trading is policed to protect research objectivity.
cards.watch: Monitoring plus, where needed, pre-approval — not an honour system.
cards.link: Conflict-of-interest theme.

recallCards.front: No separate registration if already IA/CRA/FME
recallCards.back: Existing registrants issuing public research aren't forced into a second registration.
Research must be insulated from the pressures of the entity's other lines.
Analyst personal trading is policed to protect research objectivity.

cards.title: What binds everyone
cards.law: Common Core: registration (Reg 4), net worth framework (Reg 7), fit-and-proper and PO/CO (Reg 8-9), Schedule II Part A conduct (Reg 15), governance & resilience (Reg 16-25), inspection & enforcement (Reg 37-47).
cards.means: These bind every CMI regardless of category — the shared spine.
cards.watch: Part A conduct and Chapter III obligations are common; don't mistake them for category quirks.
cards.link: Modules 1-6.

cards.title: What is category-specific
cards.law: Category specifics: distinct net-worth figures (Schedule I), Chapter IV obligations (Reg 26-36) and Schedule II Part B codes — e.g., IA fee-only rule, DP daily reconciliation, DT nominee director, IB promoter-marketing limit, CRA rating monitoring.
cards.means: Each category drags along its own obligations that do NOT bind the others.
cards.watch: The liquid-assets net-worth definition is entity-specific (only BD/CM/IB).
cards.link: Modules 7-16.

cards.title: Tag every obligation A or B
cards.law: For any obligation, ask: is it in the Common Core (binds all) or a Chapter IV / Part B / Schedule I category rule (binds one)?
cards.means: A simple, repeatable classification that prevents both over- and under-compliance.
cards.watch: Unified registration makes this tagging more important, not less.
cards.link: Ties the whole course together.

questions.title: Which of these is a COMMON obligation binding every CMI?
questions.question: Which of these is a COMMON obligation binding every CMI?

options.text: Reconciling records with the depository daily
Maintaining the Schedule II Part A code of conduct
Acting in a fiduciary capacity and receiving no third-party remuneration
Appointing a nominee director on two consecutive interest defaults

questions.question: Meridian Capital (BD + IB + distributor desks; group custody desk) makes four compliance calls. Which is WRONG?

options.text: Treats the IA fee-only rule as binding on its distributor desk
Applies Schedule II Part A conduct across all of its desks
Runs the group custody desk segregated from the other desks
Computes its net worth on the highest-of basis, not the sum

Authorised FME, Registered FME and Exempted FME, based on the investors served
Authorised FME (Retail), Authorised FME (Non-Retail) and Branch FME

Launch exchange traded funds and retail schemes, and act as investment manager for private placements of REITs and InvITs
Offer Portfolio Management Services (including for a multi-family office) and act as investment manager for private placements of REITs and InvITs
Manage a Family Investment Fund for a Single Family and offer Portfolio Management Services to accredited investors only

activities.title: Branch Net Worth
activities.question: An FME operating as a branch in IFSC satisfies the minimum net worth requirement:

options.text: By ring-fencing the full amount in a bank account maintained with a banking unit in the IFSC
At the parent level, with the parent ensuring adequate funds for the branch's day-to-day operations
At the parent level, provided the parent is regulated in a jurisdiction having an arrangement with IFSCA
At the branch level only, computed separately from the parent and certified by its auditors annually

activities.question: Learn the concepts
activities.explanation: Concepts learned. Fixed +15 XP on completion; lessons carry no right or wrong and never affect accuracy.

cards.title: Two people every FME must have
cards.law: Every FME appoints a Principal Officer — responsible overall for fund management, risk management and compliance — and an additional KMP designated as Compliance Officer.
cards.means: The PO is the apex accountable human; the CO is the professional conscience. Between them, everything the FME does has a name attached to it.
cards.trip: The 2022 regulations called the second KMP the "Compliance and Risk Manager". The 2025 text renamed it Compliance Officer. Old study material will betray you here.
cards.hook: PO owns everything; CO watches everything.

cards.title: The CO reports past the PO
cards.law: The Compliance Officer is a senior officer reporting to the board of directors — or the head of the organisation where there is no board.
cards.means: Independence is hard-wired: the person monitoring compliance does not report to the person running the funds. The CO must also be capable of understanding financial statements and the regulatory requirements.
cards.trip: 2022 said "financially literate and capable of appreciating"; 2025 sharpened it to "capable of understanding the financial statements". Small words, favourite trap.

cards.title: When two KMPs become three
cards.law: A Retail FME appoints an additional fund-management KMP BEFORE filing the offer document of its first retail scheme or ETF. Any FME crossing USD 1 billion AUM at FY-close (excluding FoF AUM) does the same.
cards.means: Scale and public money both demand a dedicated fund-management brain, separate from the PO.
cards.trip: The USD 1bn test EXCLUDES fund of funds AUM — those assets are managed at the underlying level. And the retail trigger is pre-FILING, not pre-launch.
cards.hook: Retail or a billion — either way, a third KMP.
cards.link: FoF look-through logic returns in valuation and custody (Module 9).

cards.title: Fit and proper — always, everyone
cards.law: The applicant, PO, directors/partners, KMPs and controlling shareholders must be fit and proper at all times: financial integrity, good reputation and character, honesty.
cards.means: Three positive limbs, applied continuously, to everyone who matters. A conviction involving moral turpitude or an economic offence breaks it.
cards.trip: The January 2026 Amendment rebuilt the KMP experience routes: 5 years base, 3 years with a professional qualification, and 2/3-year certification paths. If you learned the old Reg. 7 experience rules, relearn them.

activities.title: A candidate KMP holds a professional qualification and four years' rel
activities.question: A candidate KMP holds a professional qualification and four years' relevant experience. For a role under sub-regulation (2), the compliance officer should conclude that the candidate:

options.text: Qualifies, because the professional-qualification route reduces the requirement to three years
Falls short, because the base requirement of five years applies to every KMP role
Qualifies only after obtaining the certification prescribed by the Authority as well
Falls short, because professional qualifications count only towards the certification route

activities.explanation: The first proviso to Reg. 7(5)(b) reduces the requirement to three years where the KMP holds a professional qualification. Four years therefore suffices. The five-year figure is the base rule, and the certification route is a separate alternative rather than an additional condition.

activities.title: An FME registered in the IFSC also carries on a separate regulated act
activities.question: An FME registered in the IFSC also carries on a separate regulated activity outside the IFSC for which it maintains net worth. On the FME net worth requirement, the correct view is that it:

options.text: May be met by the same net worth, provided the aggregate exceeds both thresholds
Must be met separately, being additional to net worth held for any other activity
May be met by the parent, provided the parent is regulated in its home jurisdiction
Must be met separately only where the other activity is carried on within the IFSC

activities.explanation: Reg. 8(3) makes the FME requirement separate from and in addition to net worth required for other activities, whether inside or outside the IFSC. Double-counting the same capital is the error the provision exists to prevent.

activities.title: An FME proposes that its Principal Officer also act as Compliance Offi
activities.question: An FME proposes that its Principal Officer also act as Compliance Officer to keep headcount lean. The compliance risk here is that:

options.text: The Principal Officer must be resident in India while the Compliance Officer need not be
The Authority requires a minimum of four key managerial personnel in every registered FME
The roles carry distinct responsibilities and the Compliance Officer reports to the board
The Principal Officer is responsible only for fund management, not for compliance oversight

activities.explanation: The Principal Officer carries overall responsibility for the FME's activities, while the Compliance Officer reports to the board (or the head of the organisation). Collapsing the roles removes the independent reporting line that the structure is designed to create.

cards.title: Who gets in — and how many
cards.law: A VC scheme shall not have more than fifty (50) investors; non-accredited investors invest at least USD 250,000; FME employees/directors at USD 60,000.
cards.means: An exclusive room: 50 sophisticated cheques maximum. The 250K ticket is the sophistication filter; accredited investors skip it.
cards.trip: "At least" 250K — exactly 250K qualifies (2022 said "above"). And 2022 capped at 49 investors ("less than fifty"). Both flipped in 2025. Joint investors combining to 250K: only spouse, parent, or child.
cards.hook: 50 doors, 250K key, 60K staff entrance.

cards.title: The size of the pool
cards.law: Minimum corpus USD 3 Million; total corpus shall not exceed USD 200 Million.
cards.means: Both a floor and a ceiling — VC is the only mainstream scheme with a cap. Bigger ambitions route through restricted schemes.
cards.trip: Restricted schemes share the 3M floor but have NO ceiling. Don’t transplant the 200M cap.
cards.link: The 3M floor returns with new teeth in Module 4 — the 2026 unlisted gate.

cards.title: The 80/10 rule — keeping venture "venture"
cards.law: At least 80% of corpus goes to investee companies within 10 years of incorporation (or schemes meeting that test).
cards.means: Four-fifths of the money must reach genuinely young companies. This is what stops a VC label on a late-stage PE fund.
cards.trip: Ten years from INCORPORATION of the investee — not from its funding round, not from scheme launch.
cards.hook: 80% young blood, 20% free play.

cards.title: Skin in the game
cards.law: FME/associate invests ≥2.5% of targeted corpus (≤USD 30M schemes) or ≥USD 750,000 (>USD 30M), never exceeding 10%.
cards.means: The manager eats its own cooking. The floor aligns incentives; the 10% ceiling stops the FME dominating its own fund.
cards.trip: USD 750,000 is just 2.5% of 30M, frozen. And relocated schemes (moving to IFSC from abroad) are exempt entirely.
cards.hook: 750K = 2.5% of 30M, frozen.

cards.title: Conflicts and rhythm
cards.law: Associate investments need prior approval of 75% of investors by value. NAV at least annually, documented methodology; valuation by independents; leverage as disclosed in the PPM.
cards.means: Conflicted deals are democratised, not banned. And the compliance rhythm is annual — venture portfolios don’t need daily NAVs, they need methodological discipline.
cards.trip: 75% by VALUE, PRIOR — ratification after the cheque doesn’t cure it. And "VC schemes can’t borrow" is a myth: leverage is a disclosure matter.
cards.hook: 75%-by-value is the regulations’ answer to every conflict — remember it once, use it everywhere.
cards.link: The same 75% lever: restricted-scheme associate trades (Module 4) and winding-up votes (Module 11).

activities.title: A venture capital scheme has 48 investors and wishes to admit 4 more,
activities.question: A venture capital scheme has 48 investors and wishes to admit 4 more, each investing USD 300,000. The compliance officer should identify that:

options.text: The additional investors are permissible because each exceeds the USD 250,000 minimum
The scheme may admit them only after converting into a restricted scheme structure
The ceiling applies to accredited investors only, so the admissions are unaffected
Admitting all four would breach the fifty-investor ceiling applicable to VC schemes

activities.explanation: The ticket size is satisfied, but the investor ceiling for a VC scheme is fifty. Admitting four more would take the scheme to fifty-two. Meeting one condition does not cure a breach of another — the classic error in scheme structuring.

activities.title: Episode 2: The Eager Open-End
activities.question: What's wrong here?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — the scheme remains comfortably within the 25% cap on unlisted securities that applies to open-ended restricted schemes
The 25% cap is satisfied, but post the 2026 Amendment an open-ended scheme cannot touch unlisted securities until it achieves USD 3 Million corpus
The scheme could not have commenced any investment activity at all until it had first reached the USD 3 Million minimum corpus required
Open-ended restricted schemes are never permitted to invest in unlisted securities at all, whatever the size of the corpus they have raised

activities.explanation:
The 2026 Amendment layered a corpus gate under the existing 25% cap: open-ended restricted schemes must first achieve USD 3 Million before any unlisted-securities deployment.
1. The unlisted gate: The proviso inserted in Reg. 35(1) by the 2026 Amendment (w.e.f. 30.01.2026) permits unlisted-securities investment by an open-ended scheme only upon achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus. At USD 1.4 Million, the gate is shut — the 21% deployment is a breach regardless of the 25% cap.
2. What the scheme COULD do: Commencing investment activities at USD 1.4 Million was itself fine — Reg. 35(2) permits commencement at USD 1 Million, with USD 3 Million to be achieved within 12 months. The restriction is specific to unlisted securities.
3. The CO's incomplete test: Checking only the 25% cap is the pre-amendment reflex. Post-30.01.2026 the analysis is two-step: (i) has the scheme achieved USD 3M? If not, zero unlisted exposure; (ii) if yes, stay within 25% of corpus.

activities.title: Learn the concepts
activities.question: Learn the concepts
activities.explanation: Concepts learned. Fixed +15 XP on completion; lessons carry no right or wrong and never affect accuracy.

cards.title: The bigger tent
cards.law: Restricted schemes may have up to 1,000 investors. Schemes filed as Category I and II AIFs must be close-ended; Category III may be open- or close-ended.
cards.means: Twenty times the VC room, same sophistication filter (private placement to accredited/threshold investors). Structure follows strategy: locked capital for illiquid Cat I/II plays; open-ended only for Cat III.
cards.trip: The 50-investor cap is VC-only. Retail schemes have no cap at all. Keep the three numbers separate: 50 / 1,000 / unlimited.
cards.hook: 50 → 1,000 → ∞ as you climb the scheme ladder.

cards.title: Start small, prove yourself
cards.law: An open-ended restricted scheme may commence investing at USD 1 Million, achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus within 12 months.
cards.means: A two-step launch ladder: start at 1M, prove you can reach 3M within a year of the taken-on-record communication.
cards.trip: Post the January 2026 Amendment, unlisted securities are OFF-LIMITS until the 3M is actually achieved — commencing at 1M does not open the unlisted door.
cards.hook: 1M to start, 3M to touch unlisted.

cards.title: The 25% unlisted cap
cards.law: Open-ended restricted schemes cap unlisted securities at 25% of corpus — with a look-through exception for FoFs whose underlying open-ended schemes each respect the cap.
cards.means: Redemption liquidity and illiquid paper don’t mix, so open-ended structures get a hard limit. Close-ended schemes face no such cap.
cards.trip: The post-2026 test is TWO-step: (1) corpus ≥ 3M? If no — zero unlisted. (2) If yes — stay within 25%. Checking only the cap is the pre-amendment reflex.

cards.title: Doubled skin for open doors
cards.law: Close-ended: ≥2.5% or ≥USD 750K (>30M). Open-ended: ≥5% or ≥USD 1.5M (>30M). Both capped at 10%.
cards.means: When investors can redeem, manager-investor misalignment bites harder — so open-ended floors are exactly double the close-ended ones.
cards.trip: Same 750K logic as VC, but the open-ended big-scheme floor is 1.5M. Four numbers, one pattern: close 2.5%/750K, open 5%/1.5M.
cards.hook: Open-ended = close-ended × 2.

cards.title: Conflicted trades and co-investments
cards.law: Buying/selling from associates, other schemes, or a 50%+ committed investor needs 75%-by-value approval — EXCLUDING the conflicted investor’s votes. Co-investment via segregated portfolios must never be on more favourable terms than the common portfolio; SPV leverage as disclosed.
cards.means: The supermajority returns, now with a twist: the mega-investor whose trade it is doesn’t get to vote on it. And co-investors may get access, never advantage.
cards.trip: "Not more favourable" — identical terms are fine, better terms are the breach.

activities.title: A restricted scheme proposes to buy an asset from an investor holding
activities.question: A restricted scheme proposes to buy an asset from an investor holding 55% of its commitments. Approval is obtained from 78% of investors by value, counting that investor's vote. The position is that:

options.text: The approval is valid, since the 75% threshold by value has clearly been exceeded
The approval is invalid, since such transactions require unanimous investor consent
The approval is valid, provided the transaction is disclosed in the next annual report
The approval is invalid, since the interested investor's votes must be excluded

activities.explanation: Reg. 35(4) requires 75% approval by value excluding the votes of the investor concerned. Counting the 55% investor's own vote inflates the tally — the exclusion is precisely what makes the safeguard meaningful.

questions.title: Episode 2: The Eager Open-End
questions.question: What's wrong here?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — the scheme remains comfortably within the 25% cap on unlisted securities that applies to open-ended restricted schemes
The 25% cap is satisfied, but post the 2026 Amendment an open-ended scheme cannot touch unlisted securities until it achieves USD 3 Million corpus
The scheme could not have commenced any investment activity at all until it had first reached the USD 3 Million minimum corpus required
Open-ended restricted schemes are never permitted to invest in unlisted securities at all, whatever the size of the corpus they have raised

questions.explanation:
The 2026 Amendment layered a corpus gate under the existing 25% cap: open-ended restricted schemes must first achieve USD 3 Million before any unlisted-securities deployment.
1. The unlisted gate: The proviso inserted in Reg. 35(1) by the 2026 Amendment (w.e.f. 30.01.2026) permits unlisted-securities investment by an open-ended scheme only upon achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus. At USD 1.4 Million, the gate is shut — the 21% deployment is a breach regardless of the 25% cap.
2. What the scheme COULD do: Commencing investment activities at USD 1.4 Million was itself fine — Reg. 35(2) permits commencement at USD 1 Million, with USD 3 Million to be achieved within 12 months. The restriction is specific to unlisted securities.
3. The CO's incomplete test: Checking only the 25% cap is the pre-amendment reflex. Post-30.01.2026 the analysis is two-step: (i) has the scheme achieved USD 3M? If not, zero unlisted exposure; (ii) if yes, stay within 25% of corpus.

activities.title: Episode 3: The Nineteen-Day Launch
activities.question: How many compliance failures can you count?

options.text: None — nineteen working days is sufficient and trustee approval is indeed not required here
One — only the filing timeline falls short of what the regulation actually requires
Two — the filing timeline and the deferred incorporation of the Authority's comments
Three — the timeline, the deferred comments, and the missing fiduciary approval are all breaches.

activities.explanation:
Retail launch discipline is a three-lock gate: 21 working days' prior filing, comments incorporated pre-launch, and fiduciary approval before filing. Miss any one and the launch is bad.
1. Nineteen is not twenty-one: Reg. 43(1): no retail scheme launches unless the draft offer document was filed at least 21 working days before launch, with fees. Nineteen working days fails the gate — the launch date must move.
2. Comments precede launch: Reg. 43(3): the FME must ensure IFSCA's comments are incorporated in the offer document prior to launch — not in a post-launch reprint. Launching on the uncorrected document is a distinct breach.
3. Fiduciary approval is mandatory: Reg. 43(5): no retail scheme may even be filed with the Authority unless approved by the fiduciaries (here, the trustees). "For information" circulation is not approval — and this defect infects the filing itself.

cards.title: Public money, prior review
cards.law: No retail scheme launches unless the draft offer document was filed with IFSCA at least 21 working days before launch, with fees; Authority comments must be incorporated BEFORE launch.
cards.means: Private placements get a green channel; public money gets a runway. The regulator reads before the public buys.
cards.trip: WORKING days, not calendar days — 19 working days is a breach, not a rounding error. Validity: 12 months from taken-on-record.

cards.title: The 20/25 rule

cards.means: Genuine pooling, not one whale wearing a retail costume. The 6-month cure window makes the rule practical: a 30% investor at closing is curable, not fatal.
cards.trip: Contrast the logic: VC/restricted CAP investors (exclusivity); retail sets a FLOOR (genuine distribution).
cards.hook: 20 in the room, no one over a quarter.

cards.title: Form and fiduciaries

cards.trip: No LLP option for retail schemes — the one legal form the framework withholds. "Circulated to trustees for information" is not approval.
cards.link: Fiduciary duties live in the Third Schedule Part B — Module 10 territory.

cards.title: Time and the exit door

cards.trip: The extra Authority layer is the retail signature — spot it and you can reverse-engineer which scheme type a question is about.

The filing is premature, because fiduciary approval must precede the filing itself
The filing is defective only if the Authority's comments are not incorporated in time
The timeline should be 21 calendar days, so the filing is in fact earlier than required

questions.title: Episode 3: The Nineteen-Day Launch
questions.question: How many compliance failures can you count?

options.text: None — nineteen working days is sufficient and trustee approval is indeed not required here
One — only the filing timeline falls short of what the regulation actually requires
Two — the filing timeline and the deferred incorporation of the Authority's comments
Three — the timeline, the deferred comments, and the missing fiduciary approval are all breaches.

questions.explanation:
Retail launch discipline is a three-lock gate: 21 working days' prior filing, comments incorporated pre-launch, and fiduciary approval before filing. Miss any one and the launch is bad.
1. Nineteen is not twenty-one: Reg. 43(1): no retail scheme launches unless the draft offer document was filed at least 21 working days before launch, with fees. Nineteen working days fails the gate — the launch date must move.
2. Comments precede launch: Reg. 43(3): the FME must ensure IFSCA's comments are incorporated in the offer document prior to launch — not in a post-launch reprint. Launching on the uncorrected document is a distinct breach.
3. Fiduciary approval is mandatory: Reg. 43(5): no retail scheme may even be filed with the Authority unless approved by the fiduciaries (here, the trustees). "For information" circulation is not approval — and this defect infects the filing itself.

activities.title: What Makes a Fund of Funds
activities.question: A "fund of funds scheme" invests in other schemes (in IFSC, India or foreign jurisdictions), except to the extent of funds needed for:

options.text: Up to 49% of the corpus may be invested directly in the securities of listed and unlisted companies
Seed investments made in new schemes launched by its own FME, as disclosed to the investors
Meeting expenses, hedging, or liquidity for repurchases, redemptions and distributions, as disclosed in the PPM
Any purpose approved by the fiduciaries of the scheme and duly recorded in their minutes

activities.explanation: The definitional carve-outs are narrow and disclosure-bound: expenses, hedging, and redemption/distribution liquidity. Beyond those, a FoF holds schemes — not direct securities.

activities.title: A Registered FME (Non-Retail) proposes an unlisted ETF marketed only t
activities.question: A Registered FME (Non-Retail) proposes an unlisted ETF marketed only to accredited investors. The compliance officer should identify that:

options.text: Only the listing is defective, since any Registered FME may launch an ETF
Only the category is defective, since accredited-investor ETFs need not be listed
Both the category and the listing are defective, whatever the investor profile
Neither is defective, provided the offer document discloses the absence of listing

activities.explanation: Reg. 61(1) confines ETFs to a Registered FME (Retail), and Reg. 61(5) makes listing mandatory. Restricting the offer to accredited investors does not relax either requirement — investor sophistication is not a substitute for category or listing.

questions.question: A "fund of funds scheme" invests in other schemes (in IFSC, India or foreign jurisdictions), except to the extent of funds needed for:

options.text: Up to 49% of the corpus may be invested directly in the securities of listed and unlisted companies
Seed investments made in new schemes launched by its own FME, as disclosed to the investors

cards.title: Two lanes for Investment Trusts
cards.law: Private placement: at least USD 250,000 per investor or accredited investors, maximum 50 — final placement memorandum filed within 10 working days of allotment. Public offers run the full review cycle.
cards.means: REITs and InvITs mirror the scheme logic: a fast sophisticated lane with post-facto filing, and a slow public lane with pre-facto everything.
cards.trip: The private lane’s thresholds are the VC scheme’s thresholds — 250K and 50. The framework reuses its own furniture.
cards.hook: Private REIT lane = VC math: 250K, cap 50.
cards.link: Who manages them? Private placements — Non-Retail FMEs; public offers — Retail FMEs (Module 1’s activity matrix).

cards.title: The public lane, step by step
cards.law: Draft offer document ≥30 working days before the formal filing; public comments ≥14 days on four websites; due diligence certificate by the IM or investment banker; Authority observations within 30 working days of filing or 21 from a satisfactory reply — whichever is LATER.
cards.means: A public offer is a sequence of checkpoints, each with an owner and a clock. The "whichever is later" formula means sloppy query responses restart the regulator’s clock, never shorten it.
cards.trip: The comment window is 14 DAYS; the draft filing runway is 30 WORKING days. Mixing the units is the classic error.
cards.hook: 30wd draft → 14d comments → observations (30wd/21wd, later wins).

cards.title: Last gates and shelf life
cards.law: Final offer document filed with exchange(s) and Authority ≥5 working days before opening. The offer must be made within 1 year of observations — else file a fresh draft.
cards.means: A five-day final buffer, and a 12-month expiry on the regulator’s green light. Market disclosures go stale; the framework refuses to let last year’s review bless this year’s offer.
cards.trip: Miss the 1-year window and there’s no confirmatory-letter shortcut — the entire draft-and-observation cycle restarts.

questions.title: Private Placement of an Investment Trust

options.text: Investors investing at least USD 250,000 or accredited investors, capped at fifty (50) investors
Any investors at all, subject only to an overall cap of two hundred (200) investors
Institutional investors only, subject to an overall cap of one thousand investors
Accredited investors only, with no cap at all on the number of such investors

questions.question: IFSCA communicates its observations on a public-issue offer document within:

options.text: A fixed thirty (30) calendar days running from the date of the original filing
30 working days from filing, or 21 working days from satisfactory reply to queries — whichever is later
Fifteen (15) working days from the close of the public comment period itself
Sixty (60) days from the filing, extendable once at the Authority's discretion

questions.explanation: Reg. 94(e): the "whichever is later" formulation means the clock restarts with each round of queries — incomplete responses extend, not shorten, the timeline.

questions.title: An Investment Trust raises funds privately from 45 investors, of whom
questions.question: An Investment Trust raises funds privately from 45 investors, of whom 40 invest USD 300,000 each and 5 are accredited investors investing USD 100,000 each. The position is that:

options.text: The placement is compliant on both the investor count and the investment thresholds
The placement is defective, because every investor must invest at least USD 250,000
The placement is defective, because accredited investors cannot be counted separately
The placement is compliant only if the five accredited investors are institutions

questions.explanation: Reg. 93 permits investors investing at least USD 250,000 OR accredited investors, capped at fifty. Forty-five investors, with the smaller tickets coming from accredited investors, satisfies both limbs — the two categories are alternatives, not cumulative conditions.

activities.title: Where the Custodian Sits
activities.question: The custodian appointed under Reg. 132 must be based in IFSC, unless:

options.text: The parent of the fund management entity is a foreign bank regulated in its home jurisdiction and the securities are held there
The scheme invests only in securities listed on Indian stock exchanges, in which case an India-regulated custodian may be appointed
Local law where the securities are issued mandates a local custodian — a custodian regulated in that jurisdiction may then be appointed for them
The custodian fee payable would exceed the cap specified by the Authority, in which case a foreign custodian may be appointed instead

activities.explanation: Explanation I: IFSC-domicile is the default; the carve-out follows mandatory local-custody laws of the issuing jurisdiction, with information arrangements for IFSCA.

Twelve (12) months from the taken-on-record date, with no interim arrangement permitted

cards.title: Who must have a custodian
cards.law: Independent custodian mandatory for: retail schemes; open-ended restricted schemes; and any scheme with AUM above USD 70 Million. FoF exemption where underlying schemes have custodians.
cards.means: Three triggers — public money, redemption pressure, and sheer size. Miss all three and custody is your choice, not your obligation.
cards.trip: The USD 70M trigger catches CLOSE-ended restricted schemes too, once they grow. "We’re close-ended so no custodian" is only half a rule.
cards.hook: Retail, open-ended, or 70M+ — any one triggers custody.

cards.title: Where the custodian sits — and the 24-month runway
cards.law: The custodian must be IFSC-based, except where local laws of the issuing jurisdiction mandate local custody. The 2026 Amendment gives 24 months (from 30.01.2026) to make the IFSC appointment, with regulated India/foreign custodians permitted in the interim.
cards.means: Onshoring custody to GIFT City, with a realistic transition. The local-law carve-out follows mandatory foreign rules, with information arrangements for IFSCA.
cards.trip: The old Explanation II was substituted — if your compliance calendar still shows the pre-2026 transition, it’s wrong.

cards.hook: Admin, custodian, CRA, IBBI valuer — the only four.

cards.means: One 4-month clock for both audiences, an auditor test stricter than mere independence, and a monthly transparency baseline.
cards.trip: "Not in any way associated" closes side-relationship loopholes that ordinary independence tests miss.

cards.trip: "Not in any way associated" closes side-relationship loopholes that ordinary independence tests miss.

questions.title: Liability That Survives Exit
questions.question: Under the Code of Conduct, the FME, its directors, partners and officers:

options.text: Are not absolved of liability to the scheme or investors for acts of commission or omission — notwithstanding any contract or termination
Are released from all liability on resignation, provided that thirty days' notice has been duly given
May contract out of that liability with the written consent of the scheme's investors obtained in advance
Are liable only for so long as they continue to hold office within the FME or the scheme concerned

activities.title: The 2026 Winding-Up Addition
activities.question: The ground inserted by the 2026 Amendment permits winding up where:

options.text: The net asset value of the scheme falls by fifty per cent within a single quarter, measured against the previous quarter end
Funds were raised but the minimum corpus was missed within the (extended) PPM validity, and the FME did not extend it by filing and paying the fee
The custodian appointed for the scheme resigns and no replacement custodian is appointed within the prescribed period
Two consecutive annual reports of the scheme carry a qualified opinion from the statutory auditor

activities.explanation: Reg. 131(1)(c) (w.e.f. 30.01.2026) pairs with the new multi-extension regime: where a raise falls short and the FME has NOT filed for a further extension, there is now a clean statutory exit. The same amendment also inserted Reg. 131(1)(d) — a separate ground for winding up where NO investors have been onboarded and NO funds collected, and the FME voluntarily desires to wind up. Keep the two apart: (c) is a failed raise; (d) is a scheme that never started.

activities.title: Learn the concepts
activities.question: Learn the concepts
activities.explanation: Concepts learned. Fixed +15 XP on completion; lessons carry no right or wrong and never affect accuracy.

cards.title: Transparency on a monthly clock
cards.law: Investors get holding statements at the end of every month, and within 10 working days on request. Fiduciaries must disclose anything with an adverse bearing on investments.
cards.means: The baseline rhythm of investor communication — monthly by default, 10 working days on demand, and bad news travels without being asked.
cards.trip: MONTHLY holdings vs ANNUAL reports (4 months, Module 9) — two different clocks, commonly swapped in questions.
cards.hook: Holdings monthly; accounts yearly.

cards.title: Inspection — no trigger needed
cards.law: The Authority may appoint an Inspecting Authority suo motu, or on information or complaint, at ANY time — covering books, records, documents, infrastructure, procedures, systems, and associated entities. Everyone — PO, partners, trustees, directors, KMPs, employees, agents — must assist and give reasonable premises access.
cards.means: Inspection is not an event that requires cause; it’s a standing possibility. The cooperation duty reaches every human connected to the FME, down to agents.
cards.trip: "Only after a show-cause notice" is wrong; "only the compliance officer must cooperate" is wrong. No trigger, no narrow net.
cards.hook: Any time, anyone, everything.

cards.title: Winding up — three roads and a regulator’s hammer
cards.law: Grounds: tenure over; 75% of investors by value resolve; or (post-2026) funds raised but minimum corpus missed within the extended validity and the FME opts to wind up voluntarily. The Authority may also DIRECT winding up, merge schemes, or hand an FME’s schemes to ANOTHER FME to manage.
cards.means: Exit is as regulated as entry. The 2026 ground gives failed raises a clean statutory door. And the directive power to transplant scheme management is IFSC’s resolution mechanism for failing managers.
cards.trip: The investor vote is 75% by value — the same supermajority you’ve now seen in three modules. Retail extensions used 2/3; winding up uses 75%. Keep the fractions apart.
cards.link: That third ground exists BECAUSE of the multi-extension regime — Module 6’s asymmetry and Module 12’s tracker complete the picture.

recallCards.back: The baseline rhythm of investor communication — monthly by default, 10 working days on demand, and bad news travels without being asked.
Inspection is not an event that requires cause; it’s a standing possibility. The cooperation duty reaches every human connected to the FME, down to agents.

recallCards.front: Winding up — three roads and a regulator’s hammer
recallCards.back: Exit is as regulated as entry. The 2026 ground gives failed raises a clean statutory door. And the directive power to transplant scheme management is IFSC’s resolution mechanism for failing managers.

questions.title: The 2026 Winding-Up Addition

options.text: The net asset value of the scheme falls by fifty per cent within a single quarter, measured against the previous quarter end

The custodian appointed for the scheme resigns and no replacement custodian is appointed within the prescribed period
Two consecutive annual reports of the scheme carry a qualified opinion from the statutory auditor

questions.explanation: Reg. 131(1)(c) (w.e.f. 30.01.2026) pairs with the new multi-extension regime: where a raise falls short and the FME has NOT filed for a further extension, there is now a clean statutory exit. activities.title: Episode 1: The Expired Extension
activities.question: What's wrong here?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — the extension is valid, since a one-time six-month extension at a 50% fee remains available
Only the fee is wrong — it should have been 25% of the fresh-scheme filing fee for a first extension
The application is fatally late — it had to be filed while the PPM was still valid — and the fee and the CO's position are outdated
The scheme should simply have declared its first close at the USD 1.8 Million it had already raised

activities.explanation:
The IFSCA (Fund Management) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026 (w.e.f. 30.01.2026) replaced the one-time extension with a multi-extension regime for restricted schemes: each extension is 6 months from expiry of existing validity, the application must be filed while the PPM is still valid, and fees are 25% (first) / 50% (each subsequent) of the prevailing fresh-scheme filing fee.
1. Fatal timing lapse: The PPM validity (12 months from taken-on-record) expired on 14 February 2026. Post-amendment Reg. 35(2) requires the extension application to be filed at such time when the placement memorandum is still valid. Filed 25 February 2026 = dead on arrival.
2. Wrong fee: Under the 2026 Amendment, the first extension attracts 25% of the applicable fresh-scheme filing fee; 50% applies only to each subsequent extension. The CO applied the pre-amendment rate.
3. Outdated legal position: "One-time 6-month extension" was the pre-30.01.2026 regime. The amendment permits multiple extensions of 6 months each — but only via applications filed during validity. The CO's file note is itself evidence of stale knowledge.

activities.title: Old Law or Current Law? — KMP Experience
activities.question:
An individual with post-qualification experience of at least 2 (two) years in an eligible institution in IFSC, India or any foreign jurisdiction and who holds valid certification(s), as specified by the Authority, shall be considered eligible for the KMP referred under sub-regulation (2).

Is this the current legal position or the pre-amendment position?

options.text: 2022 Framework (Old)
2025/2026 Framework (New)

activities.explanation: Current law. The 2026 Amendment substituted clause (b) of the KMP experience requirement and introduced graded routes: 5 years' experience in an "eligible institution" (a newly defined term), reduced to 3 years where the KMP holds a professional qualification, and a 2-year post-qualification route where the individual holds Authority-specified certifications. The pre-amendment text simply required 5 years in related securities-market activities.

activities.title: Old Law or Current Law? — Custodian in IFSC
activities.question:
In case of schemes which are required to appoint a custodian in IFSC, if any agreement has been entered into with a custodian which is not based in IFSC as on the date of notification of these regulations, such schemes shall be required to transition to an IFSC-based custodian.

options.text: 2022 Framework (Old)

activities.question: A Registered FME wants to manage schemes on behalf of a foreign asset manager (a "third-party"). It must:

options.text: Simply disclose the arrangement in the placement memorandum of every scheme
Obtain a fresh FME registration under a new category created for the purpose
Seek authorisation from IFSCA under Part D of Chapter [on third-party fund management services]
Route the whole arrangement through a co-investment special purpose vehicle

activities.explanation: Part D (Reg. 107A–107D), inserted by the July 2025 Amendment (w.e.f. 30.07.2025), created a dedicated authorisation regime. activities.title: Third-Party FM — Liability
activities.question: In a third-party fund management arrangement, if the third-party indemnifies the FME fully, the FME's regulatory liability for the schemes:

options.text: Transfers to the third-party manager to the full extent of the indemnity given
Is shared proportionately between them in the manner set out in the arrangement
Ceases once the Authority has approved the third-party arrangement in writing
Continues in full — the FME remains liable notwithstanding any indemnification arrangement

activities.explanation: Reg. 107C(4) is explicit: notwithstanding any arrangement with the third-party, including indemnification, the FME continues to be liable for all obligations arising from the arrangement. Indemnities are a commercial recovery mechanism inter se — they never dilute regulatory accountability. The FME must also strengthen compliance resources commensurate to scale (Reg. 107C(2)).

A trust having an IFSC-based trustee appointed to it
A branch of the foreign third-party manager concerned

activities.title: KMP — The Certification Routes
activities.question: Post-amendment, an individual with post-qualification experience of 2 years in an eligible institution plus Authority-specified certifications is eligible as:

options.text: Any KMP of the FME
The KMP referred under sub-regulation (2) only
Principal Officer only
No KMP role — 5 years is an absolute floor

activities.explanation: The 2-year + certification route applies only to the KMP under sub-regulation (2). For KMPs under sub-regulations (1), (3) and (4), the certification route requires 3 years' post-qualification experience. Separately, a professional qualification (CA/CS/CMA-type membership) reduces the clause (b) experience requirement to 3 years for the sub-regulation (2) KMP. Three distinct relaxation tracks — map them precisely.

activities.title: Fee Base for Extensions
activities.question: The 25% / 50% extension fees are computed on:

options.text: The filing fee that the FME actually paid when the scheme was originally filed
The corpus of the scheme raised up to the date of the extension application
The applicable fee for filing a fresh scheme, as prevalent at the time of the extension
A flat amount in USD notified by the Authority at the start of every year

activities.explanation: The amended provisos peg the fee to the fresh-scheme filing fee "as may be prevalent at the time of such extension" — a floating base. If IFSCA revises its fee schedule between original filing and extension, the revised fee applies. Drafting detail, but exactly the kind examiners isolate.

cards.means: The single most examined change of the year — and its power comes from the asymmetry: everyone upgraded except the SSF.

cards.hook: 25 first, 50 after, file while alive — except SSFs.

questions.title: Episode 1: The Expired Extension
questions.question: What's wrong here?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — the extension is valid, since a one-time six-month extension at a 50% fee remains available
Only the fee is wrong — it should have been 25% of the fresh-scheme filing fee for a first extension
The application is fatally late — it had to be filed while the PPM was still valid — and the fee and the CO's position are outdated
The scheme should simply have declared its first close at the USD 1.8 Million it had already raised

questions.explanation:
The IFSCA (Fund Management) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026 (w.e.f. 30.01.2026) replaced the one-time extension with a multi-extension regime for restricted schemes: each extension is 6 months from expiry of existing validity, the application must be filed while the PPM is still valid, and fees are 25% (first) / 50% (each subsequent) of the prevailing fresh-scheme filing fee.
1. Fatal timing lapse: The PPM validity (12 months from taken-on-record) expired on 14 February 2026. Post-amendment Reg. 35(2) requires the extension application to be filed at such time when the placement memorandum is still valid. Filed 25 February 2026 = dead on arrival.
2. Wrong fee: Under the 2026 Amendment, the first extension attracts 25% of the applicable fresh-scheme filing fee; 50% applies only to each subsequent extension. The CO applied the pre-amendment rate.
3. Outdated legal position: "One-time 6-month extension" was the pre-30.01.2026 regime. The amendment permits multiple extensions of 6 months each — but only via applications filed during validity. The CO's file note is itself evidence of stale knowledge.

questions.title: Old Law or Current Law? — KMP Experience
questions.question:
An individual with post-qualification experience of at least 2 (two) years in an eligible institution in IFSC, India or any foreign jurisdiction and who holds valid certification(s), as specified by the Authority, shall be considered eligible for the KMP referred under sub-regulation (2).

Is this the current legal position or the pre-amendment position?

options.text: 2022 Framework (Old)
2025/2026 Framework (New)

questions.explanation: Current law. The 2026 Amendment substituted clause (b) of the KMP experience requirement and introduced graded routes: 5 years' experience in an "eligible institution" (a newly defined term), reduced to 3 years where the KMP holds a professional qualification, and a 2-year post-qualification route where the individual holds Authority-specified certifications. The pre-amendment text simply required 5 years in related securities-market activities.

questions.title: Old Law or Current Law? — Custodian in IFSC
questions.question:
In case of schemes which are required to appoint a custodian in IFSC, if any agreement has been entered into with a custodian which is not based in IFSC as on the date of notification of these regulations, such schemes shall be required to transition to an IFSC-based custodian.

Is this the current legal position or the pre-amendment position?

options.text: 2022 Framework (Old)
2025/2026 Framework (New)

questions.explanation: Pre-amendment. The 2026 Amendment substituted Explanation II to Reg. 132: schemes required to appoint an IFSC-based custodian now have a 24-month window from commencement of the Amendment (i.e., from 30.01.2026) to make that appointment, and may in the interim appoint an independent custodian in India or a foreign jurisdiction regulated by that jurisdiction's financial sector regulator.

options.text: Multiple 6-month extensions at 25%/50% fees — same as restricted schemes
A one-time option to extend by 6 months at 50% of the fresh scheme filing fee

questions.title: New Winding-Up Ground
questions.question: The January 2026 Amendment inserted a new ground for winding up a scheme. It applies where:

options.text: The FME raised funds but missed the minimum corpus within the (extended) PPM validity, and did not extend that validity by filing and paying the fee
The Authority, acting suo motu, determines that the scheme has become unviable and directs that it be wound up
Investors holding fifty per cent of the value of the scheme pass a resolution requiring it to be wound up
The net asset value of the scheme falls fifty per cent below par and the FME cannot restore it that year

The 75%-by-value investor resolution under Reg. 131(1)(b) remains separate again.
