questions.title: Third-Party FM — Liability
questions.question: In a third-party fund management arrangement, if the third-party indemnifies the FME fully, the FME's regulatory liability for the schemes:

options.text: Transfers to the third-party manager to the full extent of the indemnity given
Is shared proportionately between them in the manner set out in the arrangement
Ceases once the Authority has approved the third-party arrangement in writing
Continues in full — the FME remains liable notwithstanding any indemnification arrangement

questions.explanation: Reg. 107C(4) is explicit: notwithstanding any arrangement with the third-party, including indemnification, the FME continues to be liable for all obligations arising from the arrangement. Indemnities are a commercial recovery mechanism inter se — they never dilute regulatory accountability. The FME must also strengthen compliance resources commensurate to scale (Reg. 107C(2)).

questions.question: Post-amendment, an individual with post-qualification experience of 2 years in an eligible institution plus Authority-specified certifications is eligible as:

options.text: Any KMP of the FME
The KMP referred under sub-regulation (2) only
Principal Officer only
No KMP role — 5 years is an absolute floor

questions.explanation: The 2-year + certification route applies only to the KMP under sub-regulation (2). cards.title: “Approved” is not “notified”
cards.law: At its 29th meeting on 24 July 2026, the Authority approved a set of amendments to the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025 aimed at ease of doing business, greater disclosure and regulatory clarity.
cards.means: Approval is the decision to amend. The binding text arrives only when the amendment is notified in the Gazette. Until then, the 2025 Regulations as amended to 30 January 2026 remain the operative law — every drill in Modules 1–12 still states the law that binds you today.
cards.trip: Two opposite errors are possible. Acting on an unnotified change is a breach. Ignoring it in your planning is poor advice. A compliance officer tracks both columns.
cards.hook: Approval sets direction. Notification sets obligation.

cards.title: The contribution ceiling moves 10% → 25%
cards.law: In place of the existing 10% limit, FMEs and their associates having Indian ultimate beneficial owners will be permitted to contribute up to 25% of the corpus of VC Schemes and Restricted Schemes, where such schemes invest only in IFSC or foreign jurisdictions.
cards.means: Headroom for Indian-owned managers building an overseas track record. The floors (2.5% / 5% / USD 750K / USD 1.5M) are untouched — this raises the ceiling only, and only for a defined set.
cards.trip: It is conditional, not general: Indian UBO AND the scheme invests only in IFSC/foreign jurisdictions. Do not confuse it with the ceiling carve-out ALREADY in force under Reg. 28(1)/40 for FMEs resident outside India with no Indian UBO and not more than one-third of corpus in one investee.
cards.link: Modules 3 and 4 teach the binding 10% ceiling — that is still the examinable and enforceable figure.

cards.title: Timelines and valuation relax
cards.law: The scheme Annual Report timeline extends from four (4) to six (6) months from financial year end. Close-ended Restricted Schemes may move NAV computation and disclosure from semi-annual to annual, subject to prior approval of at least 75% of investors by value. Independent valuation is relaxed for investments in underlying scheme(s) already valued by an independent entity.
cards.means: Three operational easements. Note the middle one is not automatic — it is unlocked by an investor supermajority, the framework's recurring 75%-by-value lever.
cards.trip: Until notified, Reg. 134's four-month clock governs. Diarise four months; plan for six.
cards.link: Module 9 drills the binding four-month clock.

cards.title: New structures: blended finance
cards.law: VC Schemes and Restricted Schemes will be permitted to issue multiple classes of units with differential distribution rights — junior / subordinate classes may carry returns lower than, or bear losses higher than, their entitlement. Minimum investment in junior classes: USD 1 Million from non-individual Accredited Investors, or USD 2 Million from other investors. An ESG Scheme may accept funds as grants, subject to conditions.
cards.means: An enabling provision for blended finance — concessional or first-loss capital sitting beneath commercial capital to mobilise private money into climate and development projects.
cards.trip: The PPM must adequately and prominently disclose the classes, their distribution rights and the resulting risks; the FME and its KMPs must diligence compliance with Indian law and other Indian regulators.
cards.prov: Approved 24.07.2026 — Regulatory Framework for differential distribution
cards.hook: Junior units: USD 1Mn accredited (non-individual), USD 2Mn others.

cards.title: Investor protection tightens in parallel
cards.law: Retail offer-document disclosures expand to cover NAV computation methodology and conflicts of interest. Internal policies required under the regulations must be approved by the FME's governing body (or its delegate). Temporary deployment of monies before a scheme reaches minimum corpus will be permitted only in capital-preservation and liquidity instruments, with prior PPM/offer-document disclosure. The definition of “associate” expands to reach natural persons and non-body-corporate juridical persons holding a direct economic interest.
cards.means: Ease of business is paired with sharper governance. The wider “associate” definition matters most — it widens every conflict test that keys off that term.
cards.trip: A broader “associate” means transactions that pass your conflict screen today may need 75%-by-value investor approval once notified. Re-run the screen when it lands.

cards.title: Also approved — beyond the FM Regulations
cards.law: The Authority also approved an amendment to the IFSCA (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 on withdrawal of credit ratings by CRAs; the IFSCA (Prohibition of Market Abuse in Securities Markets) Regulations, 2026; and the IFSCA (Electronic Trading Platform) Regulations, 2026.
cards.means: The market-abuse framework is the one to watch from a fund seat: a unified regime prohibiting insider trading and fraudulent, manipulative and unfair trade practices across the IFSC securities market.
cards.trip: It is a separate regulation, not an FM Regulations amendment — but it will bind your dealing desk and your personal-trading policy all the same.

activities.title: The Ceiling That Isn’t Law Yet
activities.question: Today, an FME's contribution to its own VC scheme is capped at what share of targeted corpus?

options.text: 25%, effective from the date of the Authority meeting held on 24 July 2026
2.5%, which operates as both the floor and the ceiling for such schemes
There is no ceiling at all on an FME's contribution to a VC scheme
10% — the notified ceiling under Reg. 28(1); the approved 25% is not yet notified

activities.explanation: Reg. 28(1) caps the contribution at 10% of targeted corpus, and that is what binds until the amendment is notified. Two separate things are easily confused: (i) the ALREADY-notified carve-out disapplying the 10% ceiling where the FME and its associates are resident outside India with no Indian UBO and not more than one-third of corpus goes to one investee; and (ii) the APPROVED 25% ceiling for FMEs with Indian UBOs investing only in IFSC/foreign jurisdictions. 2.5% is the floor, not the ceiling.

activities.title: Episode 4: The Premature Ceiling
activities.provision: Reg. 28(1), Reg. 134, Reg. 26 vs approval of 24.07.2026
activities.question: How many compliance failures can you count?

options.text: None at all — the Authority has approved all three of the changes in question already
One only — the contribution percentage is premature, but the others are perfectly fine
Two — the contribution ceiling and the annual report date, but not the NAV periodicity
Three — the contribution ceiling, the NAV periodicity and the annual report date all remain governed by the notified regulations

activities.explanation:
Approval sets direction; notification sets obligation. And several approved easements are conditional rather than self-executing — the NAV relaxation needs a 75%-by-value investor vote, and the 25% ceiling needs Indian UBOs plus an IFSC/foreign-only mandate. Plan for the change, comply with the regulation.
1. The 22% contribution: Reg. 28(1) caps the FME/associate contribution at 10% of targeted corpus. The 25% ceiling was approved on 24 July 2026 but is not notified, so 22% breaches the regulation in force. Note too that even once notified, 25% is conditional — Indian ultimate beneficial owners AND a scheme investing only in IFSC or foreign jurisdictions.
2. NAV periodicity changed unilaterally: Two defects. First, the change is not yet notified. Second — and this survives notification — moving a close-ended restricted scheme from semi-annual to annual NAV requires prior approval of at least 75% of investors by value. An instruction to the fund accountant is not an investor resolution.
3. The six-month annual report diary: Reg. 134(1) requires submission not later than four months from financial year end. Diarising six months would cause the scheme to miss a statutory deadline by two months — a self-inflicted default on the strength of an unnotified amendment.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.question: Learn the concepts
lessons.explanation: Concepts learned. Fixed +15 XP on completion; lessons carry no right or wrong and never affect accuracy.

cards.title: “Approved” is not “notified”
cards.law: At its 29th meeting on 24 July 2026, the Authority approved a set of amendments to the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025 aimed at ease of doing business, greater disclosure and regulatory clarity.
cards.means: Approval is the decision to amend. The binding text arrives only when the amendment is notified in the Gazette. Until then, the 2025 Regulations as amended to 30 January 2026 remain the operative law — every drill in Modules 1–12 still states the law that binds you today.
cards.trip: Two opposite errors are possible. Acting on an unnotified change is a breach. Ignoring it in your planning is poor advice. A compliance officer tracks both columns.
cards.hook: Approval sets direction. Notification sets obligation.

cards.title: The contribution ceiling moves 10% → 25%
cards.law: In place of the existing 10% limit, FMEs and their associates having Indian ultimate beneficial owners will be permitted to contribute up to 25% of the corpus of VC Schemes and Restricted Schemes, where such schemes invest only in IFSC or foreign jurisdictions.
cards.means: Headroom for Indian-owned managers building an overseas track record. The floors (2.5% / 5% / USD 750K / USD 1.5M) are untouched — this raises the ceiling only, and only for a defined set.
cards.trip: It is conditional, not general: Indian UBO AND the scheme invests only in IFSC/foreign jurisdictions. Do not confuse it with the ceiling carve-out ALREADY in force under Reg. 28(1)/40 for FMEs resident outside India with no Indian UBO and not more than one-third of corpus in one investee.
cards.link: Modules 3 and 4 teach the binding 10% ceiling — that is still the examinable and enforceable figure.

cards.title: Timelines and valuation relax
cards.law: The scheme Annual Report timeline extends from four (4) to six (6) months from financial year end. Close-ended Restricted Schemes may move NAV computation and disclosure from semi-annual to annual, subject to prior approval of at least 75% of investors by value. Independent valuation is relaxed for investments in underlying scheme(s) already valued by an independent entity.
cards.means: Three operational easements. Note the middle one is not automatic — it is unlocked by an investor supermajority, the framework's recurring 75%-by-value lever.
cards.trip: Until notified, Reg. 134's four-month clock governs. Diarise four months; plan for six.
cards.link: Module 9 drills the binding four-month clock.

cards.title: New structures: blended finance
cards.law: VC Schemes and Restricted Schemes will be permitted to issue multiple classes of units with differential distribution rights — junior / subordinate classes may carry returns lower than, or bear losses higher than, their entitlement. Minimum investment in junior classes: USD 1 Million from non-individual Accredited Investors, or USD 2 Million from other investors. An ESG Scheme may accept funds as grants, subject to conditions.
cards.means: An enabling provision for blended finance — concessional or first-loss capital sitting beneath commercial capital to mobilise private money into climate and development projects.
cards.trip: The PPM must adequately and prominently disclose the classes, their distribution rights and the resulting risks; the FME and its KMPs must diligence compliance with Indian law and other Indian regulators.
cards.prov: Approved 24.07.2026 — Regulatory Framework for differential distribution
cards.hook: Junior units: USD 1Mn accredited (non-individual), USD 2Mn others.

cards.title: Investor protection tightens in parallel
cards.law: Retail offer-document disclosures expand to cover NAV computation methodology and conflicts of interest. Internal policies required under the regulations must be approved by the FME's governing body (or its delegate). Temporary deployment of monies before a scheme reaches minimum corpus will be permitted only in capital-preservation and liquidity instruments, with prior PPM/offer-document disclosure. The definition of “associate” expands to reach natural persons and non-body-corporate juridical persons holding a direct economic interest.
cards.means: Ease of business is paired with sharper governance. The wider “associate” definition matters most — it widens every conflict test that keys off that term.
cards.trip: A broader “associate” means transactions that pass your conflict screen today may need 75%-by-value investor approval once notified. Re-run the screen when it lands.

cards.title: Also approved — beyond the FM Regulations
cards.law: The Authority also approved an amendment to the IFSCA (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 on withdrawal of credit ratings by CRAs; the IFSCA (Prohibition of Market Abuse in Securities Markets) Regulations, 2026; and the IFSCA (Electronic Trading Platform) Regulations, 2026.
cards.means: The market-abuse framework is the one to watch from a fund seat: a unified regime prohibiting insider trading and fraudulent, manipulative and unfair trade practices across the IFSC securities market.
cards.trip: It is a separate regulation, not an FM Regulations amendment — but it will bind your dealing desk and your personal-trading policy all the same.

questions.title: The Ceiling That Isn’t Law Yet
questions.question: Today, an FME's contribution to its own VC scheme is capped at what share of targeted corpus?

options.text: 25%, effective from the date of the Authority meeting held on 24 July 2026
2.5%, which operates as both the floor and the ceiling for such schemes
There is no ceiling at all on an FME's contribution to a VC scheme
10% — the notified ceiling under Reg. 28(1); the approved 25% is not yet notified

questions.explanation: Reg. 28(1) caps the contribution at 10% of targeted corpus, and that is what binds until the amendment is notified. Two separate things are easily confused: (i) the ALREADY-notified carve-out disapplying the 10% ceiling where the FME and its associates are resident outside India with no Indian UBO and not more than one-third of corpus goes to one investee; and (ii) the APPROVED 25% ceiling for FMEs with Indian UBOs investing only in IFSC/foreign jurisdictions. 2.5% is the floor, not the ceiling.

questions.title: Approved, Not Notified — What Binds?

options.text: The approved position, from the date of the Authority meeting
Either position, at the FME's discretion, if disclosed in the PPM
The existing notified regulations — until the amendment is notified
Nothing changes until IFSCA separately issues a circular permitting reliance

questions.title: Episode 4: The Premature Ceiling
questions.provision: Reg. 28(1), Reg. 134, Reg. 26 vs approval of 24.07.2026
questions.question: How many compliance failures can you count?

options.text: None at all — the Authority has approved all three of the changes in question already
One only — the contribution percentage is premature, but the others are perfectly fine
Two — the contribution ceiling and the annual report date, but not the NAV periodicity
Three — the contribution ceiling, the NAV periodicity and the annual report date all remain governed by the notified regulations

questions.explanation:
Approval sets direction; notification sets obligation. And several approved easements are conditional rather than self-executing — the NAV relaxation needs a 75%-by-value investor vote, and the 25% ceiling needs Indian UBOs plus an IFSC/foreign-only mandate. Plan for the change, comply with the regulation.
1. The 22% contribution: Reg. 28(1) caps the FME/associate contribution at 10% of targeted corpus. The 25% ceiling was approved on 24 July 2026 but is not notified, so 22% breaches the regulation in force. Note too that even once notified, 25% is conditional — Indian ultimate beneficial owners AND a scheme investing only in IFSC or foreign jurisdictions.
2. NAV periodicity changed unilaterally: Two defects. First, the change is not yet notified. Second — and this survives notification — moving a close-ended restricted scheme from semi-annual to annual NAV requires prior approval of at least 75% of investors by value. An instruction to the fund accountant is not an investor resolution.
3. The six-month annual report diary: Reg. 134(1) requires submission not later than four months from financial year end. Diarising six months would cause the scheme to miss a statutory deadline by two months — a self-inflicted default on the strength of an unnotified amendment.

cards.title: Three doors into GIFT City fund management
cards.law: The framework recognises Authorised FMEs, Registered FMEs (Non-Retail) and Registered FMEs (Retail).
cards.means: An ascending ladder of trust. Authorised: VC schemes and single-family funds. Non-Retail adds restricted schemes, PMS and private REIT/InvIT management. Retail sits on top: retail schemes, ETFs, public REIT/InvIT offers — plus everything below.
cards.trip: Each tier inherits ALL activities of the tiers beneath it. A Retail FME never needs a second registration to run a VC scheme.
cards.hook: Think 3 doors, each opening every door before it.

cards.title: The net worth ladder
cards.law: Minimum net worth: USD 75,000 (Authorised), USD 500,000 (Non-Retail), USD 1,000,000 (Retail) — at all times.
cards.means: The price of each door. And it is a continuous obligation — dipping below the line mid-year is a breach even if you were compliant at registration.
cards.trip: Branches hold net worth at the PARENT level — but the parent must ensure the branch has operating funds. And FME net worth is separate from and additional to net worth needed for any other regulated activity.
cards.hook: 75K → 500K → 1M: roughly ×7, then ×2.

cards.title: Getting in, switching, getting out
cards.law: Deficient applications get 30 days to cure. Category change needs prior Authority approval. Surrender is effective only on acceptance.
cards.means: IFSCA controls all three gates. You cannot drift between categories by conduct, and you remain a regulated (and liable) entity until the Authority formally accepts your exit.
cards.trip: Meeting the higher net worth does NOT auto-upgrade you — Reg. 13(2) requires prior approval for any category change.
cards.link: Prior-approval logic returns for retail fiduciaries (Module 5) and business expansion (Module 11).

cards.title: Stay in your lane
cards.law: An FME shall not undertake business activities other than those specified, without prior approval of the Authority.
cards.means: The activity perimeter is closed by default. Even a branch acting on its home regulator’s approval for an outside-IFSC activity must inform IFSCA within 15 days.
cards.trip: Opening a marketing or client-service office in another jurisdiction needs PRIOR intimation — not post-facto.

cards.law: Minimum net worth: USD 75,000 (Authorised), USD 500,000 (Non-Retail), USD 1,000,000 (Retail) — at all times.
cards.means: The price of each door. And it is a continuous obligation — dipping below the line mid-year is a breach even if you were compliant at registration.
cards.trip: Branches hold net worth at the PARENT level — but the parent must ensure the branch has operating funds. And FME net worth is separate from and additional to net worth needed for any other regulated activity.
cards.hook: 75K → 500K → 1M: roughly ×7, then ×2.

cards.title: Getting in, switching, getting out
cards.law: Deficient applications get 30 days to cure. Category change needs prior Authority approval. Surrender is effective only on acceptance.
cards.means: IFSCA controls all three gates. You cannot drift between categories by conduct, and you remain a regulated (and liable) entity until the Authority formally accepts your exit.
cards.trip: Meeting the higher net worth does NOT auto-upgrade you — Reg. 13(2) requires prior approval for any category change.
cards.link: Prior-approval logic returns for retail fiduciaries (Module 5) and business expansion (Module 11).

cards.title: Stay in your lane
cards.law: An FME shall not undertake business activities other than those specified, without prior approval of the Authority.
cards.means: The activity perimeter is closed by default. Even a branch acting on its home regulator’s approval for an outside-IFSC activity must inform IFSCA within 15 days.
cards.trip: Opening a marketing or client-service office in another jurisdiction needs PRIOR intimation — not post-facto.

That the shortfall is acceptable while the FME remains profitable on a cash basis
That the FME may continue provided it restores the shortfall before the year end

"compliance officer" means any senior officer, designated so and reporting to the board of directors or head of the organization in case board is not there, who is capable of understanding the financial statements and the requirements for legal and regulatory compliance under these regulations…

Is this the 2022 definition or the current 2025 definition?

options.text: 2022 Framework (Old)

activities.title: The Principal Officer's Mandate
activities.question: The Principal Officer of an FME carries overall responsibility for:

options.text: Fund management only, with compliance resting solely with the Compliance Officer
The activities of the FME including fund management, risk management and compliance
Marketing, investor relations and distribution of the schemes under management
Custody and settlement of the assets held by each of the FME's schemes

activities.explanation: The PO is the apex accountable individual — fund management, risk management and compliance all roll up to this role. The Compliance Officer supports but does not displace PO accountability.

Only once assets under management cross USD 1 billion at a financial year end
Before launching its tenth scheme, counting both retail and non-retail schemes
Before filing with the Authority the offer document of its first retail scheme or ETF

cards.title: Two people every FME must have
cards.law: Every FME appoints a Principal Officer — responsible overall for fund management, risk management and compliance — and an additional KMP designated as Compliance Officer.
cards.means: The PO is the apex accountable human; the CO is the professional conscience. Between them, everything the FME does has a name attached to it.
cards.trip: The 2022 regulations called the second KMP the "Compliance and Risk Manager". The 2025 text renamed it Compliance Officer. Old study material will betray you here.
cards.hook: PO owns everything; CO watches everything.

cards.title: The CO reports past the PO
cards.law: The Compliance Officer is a senior officer reporting to the board of directors — or the head of the organisation where there is no board.
cards.means: Independence is hard-wired: the person monitoring compliance does not report to the person running the funds. The CO must also be capable of understanding financial statements and the regulatory requirements.
cards.trip: 2022 said "financially literate and capable of appreciating"; 2025 sharpened it to "capable of understanding the financial statements". Small words, favourite trap.

cards.title: When two KMPs become three
cards.law: A Retail FME appoints an additional fund-management KMP BEFORE filing the offer document of its first retail scheme or ETF. Any FME crossing USD 1 billion AUM at FY-close (excluding FoF AUM) does the same.
cards.means: Scale and public money both demand a dedicated fund-management brain, separate from the PO.
cards.trip: The USD 1bn test EXCLUDES fund of funds AUM — those assets are managed at the underlying level. And the retail trigger is pre-FILING, not pre-launch.
cards.hook: Retail or a billion — either way, a third KMP.
cards.link: FoF look-through logic returns in valuation and custody (Module 9).

cards.title: Fit and proper — always, everyone
cards.law: The applicant, PO, directors/partners, KMPs and controlling shareholders must be fit and proper at all times: financial integrity, good reputation and character, honesty.
cards.means: Three positive limbs, applied continuously, to everyone who matters. A conviction involving moral turpitude or an economic offence breaks it.
cards.trip: The January 2026 Amendment rebuilt the KMP experience routes: 5 years base, 3 years with a professional qualification, and 2/3-year certification paths. If you learned the old Reg. 7 experience rules, relearn them.

activities.question: A candidate KMP holds a professional qualification and four years' relevant experience. For a role under sub-regulation (2), the compliance officer should conclude that the candidate:

options.text: Qualifies, because the professional-qualification route reduces the requirement to three years
Falls short, because the base requirement of five years applies to every KMP role
Qualifies only after obtaining the certification prescribed by the Authority as well
Falls short, because professional qualifications count only towards the certification route

activities.explanation: The first proviso to Reg. 7(5)(b) reduces the requirement to three years where the KMP holds a professional qualification. Four years therefore suffices. activities.title: An FME registered in the IFSC also carries on a separate regulated act
activities.question: An FME registered in the IFSC also carries on a separate regulated activity outside the IFSC for which it maintains net worth. On the FME net worth requirement, the correct view is that it:

options.text: May be met by the same net worth, provided the aggregate exceeds both thresholds
Must be met separately, being additional to net worth held for any other activity
May be met by the parent, provided the parent is regulated in its home jurisdiction
Must be met separately only where the other activity is carried on within the IFSC

activities.explanation: Reg. 8(3) makes the FME requirement separate from and in addition to net worth required for other activities, whether inside or outside the IFSC. Double-counting the same capital is the error the provision exists to prevent.

cards.title: Two people every FME must have
cards.law: Every FME appoints a Principal Officer — responsible overall for fund management, risk management and compliance — and an additional KMP designated as Compliance Officer.
cards.means: The PO is the apex accountable human; the CO is the professional conscience. Between them, everything the FME does has a name attached to it.
cards.trip: The 2022 regulations called the second KMP the "Compliance and Risk Manager". The 2025 text renamed it Compliance Officer. Old study material will betray you here.
cards.hook: PO owns everything; CO watches everything.

cards.title: The CO reports past the PO
cards.law: The Compliance Officer is a senior officer reporting to the board of directors — or the head of the organisation where there is no board.
cards.means: Independence is hard-wired: the person monitoring compliance does not report to the person running the funds. The CO must also be capable of understanding financial statements and the regulatory requirements.
cards.trip: 2022 said "financially literate and capable of appreciating"; 2025 sharpened it to "capable of understanding the financial statements". Small words, favourite trap.

cards.title: When two KMPs become three
cards.law: A Retail FME appoints an additional fund-management KMP BEFORE filing the offer document of its first retail scheme or ETF. Any FME crossing USD 1 billion AUM at FY-close (excluding FoF AUM) does the same.
cards.means: Scale and public money both demand a dedicated fund-management brain, separate from the PO.
cards.trip: The USD 1bn test EXCLUDES fund of funds AUM — those assets are managed at the underlying level. And the retail trigger is pre-FILING, not pre-launch.
cards.hook: Retail or a billion — either way, a third KMP.
cards.link: FoF look-through logic returns in valuation and custody (Module 9).

cards.title: Fit and proper — always, everyone
cards.law: The applicant, PO, directors/partners, KMPs and controlling shareholders must be fit and proper at all times: financial integrity, good reputation and character, honesty.
cards.means: Three positive limbs, applied continuously, to everyone who matters. A conviction involving moral turpitude or an economic offence breaks it.
cards.trip: The January 2026 Amendment rebuilt the KMP experience routes: 5 years base, 3 years with a professional qualification, and 2/3-year certification paths. If you learned the old Reg. 7 experience rules, relearn them.

activities.title: VC Minimum Investment — Above or At Least?
activities.question: Under the current 2025 regulations, a non-accredited investor may invest in a Venture Capital scheme by investing:

options.text: Above USD 250,000 — strictly more than the threshold, as under the 2022 regulations
At least USD 150,000
Any amount, if the scheme has fewer than 50 investors
At least USD 250,000 — exactly USD 250,000 qualifies

cards.title: Who gets in — and how many
cards.law: A VC scheme shall not have more than fifty (50) investors; non-accredited investors invest at least USD 250,000; FME employees/directors at USD 60,000.
cards.means: An exclusive room: 50 sophisticated cheques maximum. The 250K ticket is the sophistication filter; accredited investors skip it.
cards.trip: "At least" 250K — exactly 250K qualifies (2022 said "above"). And 2022 capped at 49 investors ("less than fifty"). Both flipped in 2025. Joint investors combining to 250K: only spouse, parent, or child.
cards.hook: 50 doors, 250K key, 60K staff entrance.

cards.title: The size of the pool
cards.law: Minimum corpus USD 3 Million; total corpus shall not exceed USD 200 Million.
cards.means: Both a floor and a ceiling — VC is the only mainstream scheme with a cap. Bigger ambitions route through restricted schemes.
cards.trip: Restricted schemes share the 3M floor but have NO ceiling. Don’t transplant the 200M cap.
cards.link: The 3M floor returns with new teeth in Module 4 — the 2026 unlisted gate.

cards.title: The 80/10 rule — keeping venture "venture"
cards.law: At least 80% of corpus goes to investee companies within 10 years of incorporation (or schemes meeting that test).
cards.means: Four-fifths of the money must reach genuinely young companies. This is what stops a VC label on a late-stage PE fund.
cards.trip: Ten years from INCORPORATION of the investee — not from its funding round, not from scheme launch.
cards.hook: 80% young blood, 20% free play.

cards.title: Skin in the game
cards.law: FME/associate invests ≥2.5% of targeted corpus (≤USD 30M schemes) or ≥USD 750,000 (>USD 30M), never exceeding 10%.
cards.means: The manager eats its own cooking. The floor aligns incentives; the 10% ceiling stops the FME dominating its own fund.
cards.trip: USD 750,000 is just 2.5% of 30M, frozen. And relocated schemes (moving to IFSC from abroad) are exempt entirely.
cards.hook: 750K = 2.5% of 30M, frozen.

cards.title: Conflicts and rhythm
cards.law: Associate investments need prior approval of 75% of investors by value. NAV at least annually, documented methodology; valuation by independents; leverage as disclosed in the PPM.
cards.means: Conflicted deals are democratised, not banned. And the compliance rhythm is annual — venture portfolios don’t need daily NAVs, they need methodological discipline.
cards.trip: 75% by VALUE, PRIOR — ratification after the cheque doesn’t cure it. And "VC schemes can’t borrow" is a myth: leverage is a disclosure matter.
cards.hook: 75%-by-value is the regulations’ answer to every conflict — remember it once, use it everywhere.
cards.link: The same 75% lever: restricted-scheme associate trades (Module 4) and winding-up votes (Module 11).

activities.title: A venture capital scheme has 48 investors and wishes to admit 4 more,
activities.question: A venture capital scheme has 48 investors and wishes to admit 4 more, each investing USD 300,000. The compliance officer should identify that:

options.text: The additional investors are permissible because each exceeds the USD 250,000 minimum
The scheme may admit them only after converting into a restricted scheme structure
The ceiling applies to accredited investors only, so the admissions are unaffected
Admitting all four would breach the fifty-investor ceiling applicable to VC schemes

activities.explanation: The ticket size is satisfied, but the investor ceiling for a VC scheme is fifty. Admitting four more would take the scheme to fifty-two. Meeting one condition does not cure a breach of another — the classic error in scheme structuring.

cards.title: Who gets in — and how many
cards.law: A VC scheme shall not have more than fifty (50) investors; non-accredited investors invest at least USD 250,000; FME employees/directors at USD 60,000.
cards.means: An exclusive room: 50 sophisticated cheques maximum. The 250K ticket is the sophistication filter; accredited investors skip it.
cards.trip: "At least" 250K — exactly 250K qualifies (2022 said "above"). And 2022 capped at 49 investors ("less than fifty"). Both flipped in 2025. Joint investors combining to 250K: only spouse, parent, or child.
cards.hook: 50 doors, 250K key, 60K staff entrance.

cards.title: The size of the pool
cards.law: Minimum corpus USD 3 Million; total corpus shall not exceed USD 200 Million.
cards.means: Both a floor and a ceiling — VC is the only mainstream scheme with a cap. Bigger ambitions route through restricted schemes.
cards.trip: Restricted schemes share the 3M floor but have NO ceiling. Don’t transplant the 200M cap.
cards.link: The 3M floor returns with new teeth in Module 4 — the 2026 unlisted gate.

cards.title: The 80/10 rule — keeping venture "venture"
cards.law: At least 80% of corpus goes to investee companies within 10 years of incorporation (or schemes meeting that test).
cards.means: Four-fifths of the money must reach genuinely young companies. This is what stops a VC label on a late-stage PE fund.
cards.trip: Ten years from INCORPORATION of the investee — not from its funding round, not from scheme launch.
cards.hook: 80% young blood, 20% free play.

cards.title: Skin in the game
cards.law: FME/associate invests ≥2.5% of targeted corpus (≤USD 30M schemes) or ≥USD 750,000 (>USD 30M), never exceeding 10%.
cards.means: The manager eats its own cooking. The floor aligns incentives; the 10% ceiling stops the FME dominating its own fund.
cards.trip: USD 750,000 is just 2.5% of 30M, frozen. And relocated schemes (moving to IFSC from abroad) are exempt entirely.
cards.hook: 750K = 2.5% of 30M, frozen.

cards.title: Conflicts and rhythm
cards.law: Associate investments need prior approval of 75% of investors by value. NAV at least annually, documented methodology; valuation by independents; leverage as disclosed in the PPM.
cards.means: Conflicted deals are democratised, not banned. And the compliance rhythm is annual — venture portfolios don’t need daily NAVs, they need methodological discipline.
cards.trip: 75% by VALUE, PRIOR — ratification after the cheque doesn’t cure it. And "VC schemes can’t borrow" is a myth: leverage is a disclosure matter.
cards.hook: 75%-by-value is the regulations’ answer to every conflict — remember it once, use it everywhere.
cards.link: The same 75% lever: restricted-scheme associate trades (Module 4) and winding-up votes (Module 11).

activities.title: Episode 2: The Eager Open-End
activities.question: What's wrong here?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — the scheme remains comfortably within the 25% cap on unlisted securities that applies to open-ended restricted schemes
The 25% cap is satisfied, but post the 2026 Amendment an open-ended scheme cannot touch unlisted securities until it achieves USD 3 Million corpus
The scheme could not have commenced any investment activity at all until it had first reached the USD 3 Million minimum corpus required
Open-ended restricted schemes are never permitted to invest in unlisted securities at all, whatever the size of the corpus they have raised

activities.explanation:
The 2026 Amendment layered a corpus gate under the existing 25% cap: open-ended restricted schemes must first achieve USD 3 Million before any unlisted-securities deployment.
1. The unlisted gate: The proviso inserted in Reg. 35(1) by the 2026 Amendment (w.e.f. 30.01.2026) permits unlisted-securities investment by an open-ended scheme only upon achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus. At USD 1.4 Million, the gate is shut — the 21% deployment is a breach regardless of the 25% cap.
2. What the scheme COULD do: Commencing investment activities at USD 1.4 Million was itself fine — Reg. 35(2) permits commencement at USD 1 Million, with USD 3 Million to be achieved within 12 months. The restriction is specific to unlisted securities.
3. The CO's incomplete test: Checking only the 25% cap is the pre-amendment reflex. Post-30.01.2026 the analysis is two-step: (i) has the scheme achieved USD 3M? If not, zero unlisted exposure; (ii) if yes, stay within 25% of corpus.

cards.title: The bigger tent
cards.law: Restricted schemes may have up to 1,000 investors. Schemes filed as Category I and II AIFs must be close-ended; Category III may be open- or close-ended.
cards.means: Twenty times the VC room, same sophistication filter (private placement to accredited/threshold investors). Structure follows strategy: locked capital for illiquid Cat I/II plays; open-ended only for Cat III.
cards.trip: The 50-investor cap is VC-only. Retail schemes have no cap at all. Keep the three numbers separate: 50 / 1,000 / unlimited.
cards.hook: 50 → 1,000 → ∞ as you climb the scheme ladder.

cards.title: Start small, prove yourself
cards.law: An open-ended restricted scheme may commence investing at USD 1 Million, achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus within 12 months.
cards.means: A two-step launch ladder: start at 1M, prove you can reach 3M within a year of the taken-on-record communication.
cards.trip: Post the January 2026 Amendment, unlisted securities are OFF-LIMITS until the 3M is actually achieved — commencing at 1M does not open the unlisted door.
cards.hook: 1M to start, 3M to touch unlisted.

cards.title: The 25% unlisted cap
cards.law: Open-ended restricted schemes cap unlisted securities at 25% of corpus — with a look-through exception for FoFs whose underlying open-ended schemes each respect the cap.
cards.means: Redemption liquidity and illiquid paper don’t mix, so open-ended structures get a hard limit. Close-ended schemes face no such cap.
cards.trip: The post-2026 test is TWO-step: (1) corpus ≥ 3M? If no — zero unlisted. (2) If yes — stay within 25%. Checking only the cap is the pre-amendment reflex.

cards.title: Doubled skin for open doors
cards.law: Close-ended: ≥2.5% or ≥USD 750K (>30M). Open-ended: ≥5% or ≥USD 1.5M (>30M). Both capped at 10%.
cards.means: When investors can redeem, manager-investor misalignment bites harder — so open-ended floors are exactly double the close-ended ones.
cards.trip: Same 750K logic as VC, but the open-ended big-scheme floor is 1.5M. Four numbers, one pattern: close 2.5%/750K, open 5%/1.5M.
cards.hook: Open-ended = close-ended × 2.

cards.title: Conflicted trades and co-investments
cards.law: Buying/selling from associates, other schemes, or a 50%+ committed investor needs 75%-by-value approval — EXCLUDING the conflicted investor’s votes. Co-investment via segregated portfolios must never be on more favourable terms than the common portfolio; SPV leverage as disclosed.
cards.means: The supermajority returns, now with a twist: the mega-investor whose trade it is doesn’t get to vote on it. And co-investors may get access, never advantage.
cards.trip: "Not more favourable" — identical terms are fine, better terms are the breach.
cards.link: You met 75%-by-value in Module 3. Here it excludes the conflicted voter — the framework’s refinement for bigger rooms.

activities.title: An open-ended restricted scheme has raised USD 2.4 Million and wishes
activities.question: An open-ended restricted scheme has raised USD 2.4 Million and wishes to take a 15% position in an unlisted company. The compliance officer should advise that:

options.text: The investment is permitted, since 15% is comfortably within the 25% unlisted cap
The investment is permitted only if the unlisted company is incorporated in the IFSC
The investment must wait until the scheme achieves the USD 3 Million minimum corpus
The scheme cannot invest in unlisted securities at all while it remains open-ended

activities.explanation: The 25% cap is satisfied, but the second proviso to Reg. 35(1) inserted in 2026 bars unlisted investment altogether until the scheme achieves the USD 3 Million minimum corpus. Two separate conditions apply and both must be met.

activities.title: A restricted scheme proposes to buy an asset from an investor holding
activities.question: A restricted scheme proposes to buy an asset from an investor holding 55% of its commitments. Approval is obtained from 78% of investors by value, counting that investor's vote. The position is that:

options.text: The approval is valid, since the 75% threshold by value has clearly been exceeded
The approval is invalid, since such transactions require unanimous investor consent
The approval is valid, provided the transaction is disclosed in the next annual report
The approval is invalid, since the interested investor's votes must be excluded

activities.explanation: Reg. 35(4) requires 75% approval by value excluding the votes of the investor concerned. Counting the 55% investor's own vote inflates the tally — the exclusion is precisely what makes the safeguard meaningful.

activities.title: A close-ended restricted scheme with a targeted corpus of USD 40 Milli
activities.question: A close-ended restricted scheme with a targeted corpus of USD 40 Million proposes an FME contribution of USD 900,000. The compliance officer should identify that this:

options.text: Satisfies the floor, since USD 750,000 is the applicable minimum for close-ended schemes
Falls short, because the floor for a corpus above USD 30 Million is USD 1,500,000
Exceeds the ceiling, because contribution is capped at 2.5% of the targeted corpus
Satisfies the floor, provided the balance is contributed before the scheme's first close

activities.explanation: For close-ended restricted schemes the floor is 2.5% of targeted corpus or USD 750,000, whichever is lower. The USD 1,500,000 figure belongs to the open-ended regime under Reg. 40(b). Confusing the two floors is the common error.

questions.title: Episode 2: The Eager Open-End
questions.question: What's wrong here?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — the scheme remains comfortably within the 25% cap on unlisted securities that applies to open-ended restricted schemes
The 25% cap is satisfied, but post the 2026 Amendment an open-ended scheme cannot touch unlisted securities until it achieves USD 3 Million corpus
The scheme could not have commenced any investment activity at all until it had first reached the USD 3 Million minimum corpus required
Open-ended restricted schemes are never permitted to invest in unlisted securities at all, whatever the size of the corpus they have raised

questions.explanation:
The 2026 Amendment layered a corpus gate under the existing 25% cap: open-ended restricted schemes must first achieve USD 3 Million before any unlisted-securities deployment.
1. The unlisted gate: The proviso inserted in Reg. 35(1) by the 2026 Amendment (w.e.f. 30.01.2026) permits unlisted-securities investment by an open-ended scheme only upon achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus. At USD 1.4 Million, the gate is shut — the 21% deployment is a breach regardless of the 25% cap.
2. What the scheme COULD do: Commencing investment activities at USD 1.4 Million was itself fine — Reg. 35(2) permits commencement at USD 1 Million, with USD 3 Million to be achieved within 12 months. The restriction is specific to unlisted securities.
3. The CO's incomplete test: Checking only the 25% cap is the pre-amendment reflex. Post-30.01.2026 the analysis is two-step: (i) has the scheme achieved USD 3M? If not, zero unlisted exposure; (ii) if yes, stay within 25% of corpus.

activities.title: Episode 3: The Nineteen-Day Launch
activities.question: How many compliance failures can you count?

options.text: None — nineteen working days is sufficient and trustee approval is indeed not required here
One — only the filing timeline falls short of what the regulation actually requires
Two — the filing timeline and the deferred incorporation of the Authority's comments
Three — the timeline, the deferred comments, and the missing fiduciary approval are all breaches.

activities.explanation:
Retail launch discipline is a three-lock gate: 21 working days' prior filing, comments incorporated pre-launch, and fiduciary approval before filing. Miss any one and the launch is bad.
1. Nineteen is not twenty-one: Reg. 43(1): no retail scheme launches unless the draft offer document was filed at least 21 working days before launch, with fees. Nineteen working days fails the gate — the launch date must move.
2. Comments precede launch: Reg. 43(3): the FME must ensure IFSCA's comments are incorporated in the offer document prior to launch — not in a post-launch reprint. Launching on the uncorrected document is a distinct breach.
3. Fiduciary approval is mandatory: Reg. 43(5): no retail scheme may even be filed with the Authority unless approved by the fiduciaries (here, the trustees). "For information" circulation is not approval — and this defect infects the filing itself.

cards.title: Public money, prior review
cards.law: No retail scheme launches unless the draft offer document was filed with IFSCA at least 21 working days before launch, with fees; Authority comments must be incorporated BEFORE launch.
cards.means: Private placements get a green channel; public money gets a runway. The regulator reads before the public buys.
cards.trip: WORKING days, not calendar days — 19 working days is a breach, not a rounding error. Validity: 12 months from taken-on-record.

cards.title: The 20/25 rule
cards.law: At least 20 investors; no single investor above 25% — achieved within 6 months of closure of the offer.
cards.means: Genuine pooling, not one whale wearing a retail costume. The 6-month cure window makes the rule practical: a 30% investor at closing is curable, not fatal.
cards.trip: Contrast the logic: VC/restricted CAP investors (exclusivity); retail sets a FLOOR (genuine distribution).
cards.hook: 20 in the room, no one over a quarter.

cards.title: Form and fiduciaries

cards.trip: No LLP option for retail schemes — the one legal form the framework withholds. "Circulated to trustees for information" is not approval.
cards.link: Fiduciary duties live in the Third Schedule Part B — Module 10 territory.

cards.title: Time and the exit door

cards.means: For sophisticated schemes, investor supermajority alone extends tenure. Retail adds the regulator as a second lock.
cards.trip: The extra Authority layer is the retail signature — spot it and you can reverse-engineer which scheme type a question is about.
cards.hook: Retail = investor vote + regulator’s yes.

questions.title: Episode 3: The Nineteen-Day Launch
questions.question: How many compliance failures can you count?

options.text: None — nineteen working days is sufficient and trustee approval is indeed not required here
One — only the filing timeline falls short of what the regulation actually requires
Two — the filing timeline and the deferred incorporation of the Authority's comments
Three — the timeline, the deferred comments, and the missing fiduciary approval are all breaches.

questions.explanation:
Retail launch discipline is a three-lock gate: 21 working days' prior filing, comments incorporated pre-launch, and fiduciary approval before filing. Miss any one and the launch is bad.
1. Nineteen is not twenty-one: Reg. 43(1): no retail scheme launches unless the draft offer document was filed at least 21 working days before launch, with fees. Nineteen working days fails the gate — the launch date must move.
2. Comments precede launch: Reg. 43(3): the FME must ensure IFSCA's comments are incorporated in the offer document prior to launch — not in a post-launch reprint. Launching on the uncorrected document is a distinct breach.
3. Fiduciary approval is mandatory: Reg. 43(5): no retail scheme may even be filed with the Authority unless approved by the fiduciaries (here, the trustees). "For information" circulation is not approval — and this defect infects the filing itself.

Act as an insolvency professional in proceedings before the Tribunal itself

activities.title: Extending SSF Tenure Beyond Two Years
activities.question: Extension of an SSF's tenure beyond the initial 2-year extension requires:

options.text: A fresh two-thirds vote of the investors by value at the end of each financial year
Express consent of willing investors, with an exit opportunity for dissenting investors
The approval of the Authority alone, without any reference to the investors
Nothing further, since extension beyond that point is prohibited absolutely

activities.explanation: The ladder: up to 2 years on a 2/3-by-value vote; beyond that, only willing investors stay and dissenters must be offered an exit. Consent replaces majority coercion at the far end.

Eighteen (18) months from the launch of the scheme through to its first close
Twelve (12) months from the taken-on-record communication, within which first close must be declared

cards.title: The distressed-asset specialist
cards.law: A special situation fund invests in special situation assets and may act as a resolution applicant under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.
cards.means: The bridge between IFSC capital and Indian insolvency resolution — an SSF can walk into a CIRP and bid for the company itself.
cards.trip: Launched by a REGISTERED FME via private placement. Authorised FMEs (VC + family funds only) cannot.
cards.hook: SSF = the fund that can bid in an IBC resolution.

cards.title: Locked capital, long game
cards.law: SSFs are close-ended only, minimum tenure 3 years; extension up to 2 years with two-thirds by value; beyond that, only willing investors stay and dissenters get an exit.
cards.means: Distressed strategies and redemption liquidity are structurally incompatible. The extension ladder ends in pure consent: past year five, nobody is locked in against their will.
cards.trip: Beyond the 2-year extension it is NOT another vote — it’s express consent of the willing plus an exit for the rest.

cards.title: The extension asymmetry — 2026’s sharpest trap
cards.law: If an SSF misses its minimum corpus, it has a ONE-TIME option to extend the PPM by 6 months at 50% of the fresh-scheme fee.
cards.means: This is the pre-2026 rule — and for SSFs it still IS the rule. The January 2026 Amendment moved VC and restricted schemes to multiple extensions (25% first, 50% after, filed while the PPM is valid) but left Reg. 55(3) untouched.
cards.trip: One framework, two extension regimes. If a question doesn’t specify the scheme type, the extension answer is "it depends" — and that’s the point.
cards.hook: Everyone upgraded to multi-extension in 2026 — except the SSF.
cards.link: The full amendment mechanics live in Module 12, the Amendment Tracker.

The extension is automatic, the memorandum reviving on payment of the prescribed fee

activities.title: An Investment Trust raises funds privately from 45 investors, of whom
activities.question: An Investment Trust raises funds privately from 45 investors, of whom 40 invest USD 300,000 each and 5 are accredited investors investing USD 100,000 each. The position is that:

options.text: The placement is compliant on both the investor count and the investment thresholds
The placement is defective, because every investor must invest at least USD 250,000
The placement is defective, because accredited investors cannot be counted separately
The placement is compliant only if the five accredited investors are institutions

activities.explanation: Reg. 93 permits investors investing at least USD 250,000 OR accredited investors, capped at fifty. Forty-five investors, with the smaller tickets coming from accredited investors, satisfies both limbs — the two categories are alternatives, not cumulative conditions.

cards.trip: The USD 70M trigger catches CLOSE-ended restricted schemes too, once they grow. "We’re close-ended so no custodian" is only half a rule.
cards.hook: Retail, open-ended, or 70M+ — any one triggers custody.

cards.title: Where the custodian sits — and the 24-month runway

cards.means: Onshoring custody to GIFT City, with a realistic transition. The local-law carve-out follows mandatory foreign rules, with information arrangements for IFSCA.

cards.means: One 4-month clock for both audiences, an auditor test stricter than mere independence, and a monthly transparency baseline.
cards.trip: "Not in any way associated" closes side-relationship loopholes that ordinary independence tests miss.

cards.title: Who must have a custodian
cards.law: Independent custodian mandatory for: retail schemes; open-ended restricted schemes; and any scheme with AUM above USD 70 Million. FoF exemption where underlying schemes have custodians.
cards.means: Three triggers — public money, redemption pressure, and sheer size. Miss all three and custody is your choice, not your obligation.
cards.trip: The USD 70M trigger catches CLOSE-ended restricted schemes too, once they grow. "We’re close-ended so no custodian" is only half a rule.
cards.hook: Retail, open-ended, or 70M+ — any one triggers custody.

cards.title: Where the custodian sits — and the 24-month runway
cards.law: The custodian must be IFSC-based, except where local laws of the issuing jurisdiction mandate local custody. The 2026 Amendment gives 24 months (from 30.01.2026) to make the IFSC appointment, with regulated India/foreign custodians permitted in the interim.
cards.means: Onshoring custody to GIFT City, with a realistic transition. The local-law carve-out follows mandatory foreign rules, with information arrangements for IFSCA.
cards.trip: The old Explanation II was substituted — if your compliance calendar still shows the pre-2026 transition, it’s wrong.
cards.prov: Reg. 132 Expl. I–II, as amended w.e.f. 30.01.2026

cards.title: Valuation: named independents, one schedule
cards.law: Assets valued per Sixth Schedule norms by an independent service provider: fund administrator, custodian, Authority-registered credit rating agency, or IBBI-registered valuer. FoF look-through exemption applies.
cards.means: Not "any independent person" — a closed list of four professional categories. Norms in the Sixth Schedule; execution by the named independents; obligation shared by FME and fiduciaries.
cards.trip: "Any SEBI-registered merchant banker" or "any CA" are not on the list — favourite wrong options.
cards.hook: Admin, custodian, CRA, IBBI valuer — the only four.

cards.title: The reporting clock
cards.law: Annual report to the Authority AND abridged summary to investors within 4 months of FY-end; full report within 15 days of an investor request. Auditor must be "not in any way associated" with the FME. Monthly holding statements; 10 working days for ad hoc requests.
cards.means: One 4-month clock for both audiences, an auditor test stricter than mere independence, and a monthly transparency baseline.
cards.trip: "Not in any way associated" closes side-relationship loopholes that ordinary independence tests miss.
cards.link: These reports are exactly what the Inspecting Authority reads first — Module 11.

activities.title: Liability That Survives Exit
activities.question: Under the Code of Conduct, the FME, its directors, partners and officers:

options.text: Are not absolved of liability to the scheme or investors for acts of commission or omission — notwithstanding any contract or termination
Are released from all liability on resignation, provided that thirty days' notice has been duly given
May contract out of that liability with the written consent of the scheme's investors obtained in advance
Are liable only for so long as they continue to hold office within the FME or the scheme concerned

activities.explanation: The Code pierces both contract and exit: liability for acts while in office survives termination and cannot be waived by agreement. The FME is also responsible for acts of its employees and procured personnel.

activities.title: Episode 1: The Expired Extension
activities.question: What's wrong here?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — the extension is valid, since a one-time six-month extension at a 50% fee remains available
Only the fee is wrong — it should have been 25% of the fresh-scheme filing fee for a first extension
The application is fatally late — it had to be filed while the PPM was still valid — and the fee and the CO's position are outdated
The scheme should simply have declared its first close at the USD 1.8 Million it had already raised

activities.explanation:
The IFSCA (Fund Management) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026 (w.e.f. 30.01.2026) replaced the one-time extension with a multi-extension regime for restricted schemes: each extension is 6 months from expiry of existing validity, the application must be filed while the PPM is still valid, and fees are 25% (first) / 50% (each subsequent) of the prevailing fresh-scheme filing fee.
1. Fatal timing lapse: The PPM validity (12 months from taken-on-record) expired on 14 February 2026. Post-amendment Reg. 35(2) requires the extension application to be filed at such time when the placement memorandum is still valid. Filed 25 February 2026 = dead on arrival.
2. Wrong fee: Under the 2026 Amendment, the first extension attracts 25% of the applicable fresh-scheme filing fee; 50% applies only to each subsequent extension. The CO applied the pre-amendment rate.
3. Outdated legal position: "One-time 6-month extension" was the pre-30.01.2026 regime. The amendment permits multiple extensions of 6 months each — but only via applications filed during validity. The CO's file note is itself evidence of stale knowledge.

activities.title: Old Law or Current Law? — KMP Experience
activities.question:
An individual with post-qualification experience of at least 2 (two) years in an eligible institution in IFSC, India or any foreign jurisdiction and who holds valid certification(s), as specified by the Authority, shall be considered eligible for the KMP referred under sub-regulation (2).

Is this the current legal position or the pre-amendment position?

options.text: 2022 Framework (Old)
2025/2026 Framework (New)

activities.explanation: Current law. The 2026 Amendment substituted clause (b) of the KMP experience requirement and introduced graded routes: 5 years' experience in an "eligible institution" (a newly defined term), reduced to 3 years where the KMP holds a professional qualification, and a 2-year post-qualification route where the individual holds Authority-specified certifications. The pre-amendment text simply required 5 years in related securities-market activities.

activities.title: New Winding-Up Ground
activities.question: The January 2026 Amendment inserted a new ground for winding up a scheme. It applies where:

options.text: The FME raised funds but missed the minimum corpus within the (extended) PPM validity, and did not extend that validity by filing and paying the fee
The Authority, acting suo motu, determines that the scheme has become unviable and directs that it be wound up
Investors holding fifty per cent of the value of the scheme pass a resolution requiring it to be wound up
The net asset value of the scheme falls fifty per cent below par and the FME cannot restore it that year

activities.explanation: New Reg. 131(1)(c): an exit route where a scheme raised some money, never hit minimum corpus within validity, and the FME has not filed (with fee) for a further extension. The 2026 Amendment ALSO inserted Reg. 131(1)(d): winding up where no investors were onboarded and no funds collected, and the FME voluntarily desires to wind up. The 75%-by-value investor resolution under Reg. 131(1)(b) remains separate again.

activities.title: Custodian Transition Window
activities.question: A retail scheme required to appoint an IFSC-based custodian may, under the substituted Explanation II, make that appointment within:

options.text: Twelve (12) months from the launch of the scheme, using any independent custodian meanwhile
24 months from commencement of the 2026 Amendment, using an India/foreign-regulated custodian in the interim
No transition at all — an IFSC-based custodian is required from the very first day
Six (6) months from the filing of the placement memorandum with the Authority itself

activities.explanation: 24-month runway from 30.01.2026. During the window, the FME may appoint an independent custodian in India or any foreign jurisdiction regulated by the local financial sector regulator, with information arrangements for IFSCA. Anchor fact alongside it: Reg. 132 mandates custodians for retail schemes, open-ended restricted schemes, and all other schemes with AUM above USD 70 Million.

activities.title: Third-Party Fund Management — Gateway
activities.question: A Registered FME wants to manage schemes on behalf of a foreign asset manager (a "third-party"). It must:

options.text: Simply disclose the arrangement in the placement memorandum of every scheme
Obtain a fresh FME registration under a new category created for the purpose
Seek authorisation from IFSCA under Part D of Chapter [on third-party fund management services]
Route the whole arrangement through a co-investment special purpose vehicle

activities.explanation: Part D (Reg. 107A–107D), inserted by the July 2025 Amendment (w.e.f. 30.07.2025), created a dedicated authorisation regime. A "third-party fund manager" must itself be registered/regulated for fund management or similar activity with the financial sector regulator of its country of incorporation. The FME may continue its own schemes and PMS in parallel under its existing registration.

activities.title: Third-Party FM — Liability
activities.question: In a third-party fund management arrangement, if the third-party indemnifies the FME fully, the FME's regulatory liability for the schemes:

options.text: Transfers to the third-party manager to the full extent of the indemnity given
Is shared proportionately between them in the manner set out in the arrangement
Ceases once the Authority has approved the third-party arrangement in writing
Continues in full — the FME remains liable notwithstanding any indemnification arrangement

activities.explanation: Reg. 107C(4) is explicit: notwithstanding any arrangement with the third-party, including indemnification, the FME continues to be liable for all obligations arising from the arrangement. Indemnities are a commercial recovery mechanism inter se — they never dilute regulatory accountability. The FME must also strengthen compliance resources commensurate to scale (Reg. 107C(2)).

activities.title: Third-Party FM — Legal Form
activities.question: An FME seeking authorisation for third-party fund management services must be set up in IFSC as:

options.text: A company, LLP, or any other form permitted by the Authority
A company only, and no other legal form is permitted at all
A trust having an IFSC-based trustee appointed to it
A branch of the foreign third-party manager concerned

activities.explanation: Reg. 107D(1): company, LLP, or any other form as may be permitted by the Authority. A branch structure would sit oddly with the liability architecture of Reg. 107C(4), which presumes a substantively resourced IFSC entity.

activities.title: KMP — The Certification Routes
activities.question: Post-amendment, an individual with post-qualification experience of 2 years in an eligible institution plus Authority-specified certifications is eligible as:

options.text: Any KMP of the FME
The KMP referred under sub-regulation (2) only
Principal Officer only
No KMP role — 5 years is an absolute floor

activities.explanation: The 2-year + certification route applies only to the KMP under sub-regulation (2). For KMPs under sub-regulations (1), (3) and (4), the certification route requires 3 years' post-qualification experience. Separately, a professional qualification (CA/CS/CMA-type membership) reduces the clause (b) experience requirement to 3 years for the sub-regulation (2) KMP. Three distinct relaxation tracks — map them precisely.

activities.title: Fee Base for Extensions
activities.question: The 25% / 50% extension fees are computed on:

options.text: The filing fee that the FME actually paid when the scheme was originally filed
The corpus of the scheme raised up to the date of the extension application
The applicable fee for filing a fresh scheme, as prevalent at the time of the extension
A flat amount in USD notified by the Authority at the start of every year

activities.explanation: The amended provisos peg the fee to the fresh-scheme filing fee "as may be prevalent at the time of such extension" — a floating base. If IFSCA revises its fee schedule between original filing and extension, the revised fee applies. Drafting detail, but exactly the kind examiners isolate.

cards.title: July 2025 — third-party fund management arrives
cards.law: Part D (Reg. 107A–107D): an FME may manage schemes of third parties, with Authority authorisation; the arrangement must be in company/LLP form; and the FME’s liability is NON-DELEGABLE notwithstanding any indemnity.
cards.means: A new business line with an old principle bolted on: you can outsource the work, never the responsibility.
cards.trip: "Notwithstanding any indemnity" — the contract can shift money, not accountability.

cards.title: January 2026 — the KMP rebuild
cards.law: Reg. 7’s KMP clause (b) substituted: an eligible-institution framework with a 5-year base experience route, 3 years with a professional qualification, and 2/3-year certification routes.
cards.means: The talent gate widened — professional qualifications and certifications now buy down the experience requirement.
cards.trip: The routes differ by which KMP and which sub-regulation — precision matters more here than anywhere.
cards.link: Full detail drilled in Module 2.

cards.title: January 2026 — the extension revolution
cards.law: Reg. 19(3) and 35(2): MULTIPLE 6-month PPM extensions, applied for while the PPM is still valid — 25% of the fresh-scheme fee for the first, 50% for each subsequent. Reg. 55(3) for SSFs: UNTOUCHED (one-time, 6 months, 50%).
cards.means: The single most examined change of the year — and its power comes from the asymmetry: everyone upgraded except the SSF.
cards.trip: File WHILE VALID. A lapsed PPM cannot be revived by an extension application — the timing condition is part of the rule.
cards.hook: 25 first, 50 after, file while alive — except SSFs.

cards.title: January 2026 — gates, exits and custody clocks
cards.law: New proviso to Reg. 35(1): open-ended schemes touch unlisted securities only after achieving USD 3M corpus. New Reg. 131(1)(c): voluntary winding-up where the (extended) raise still misses minimum corpus. Reg. 132 Expl. II substituted: 24 months from 30.01.2026 to appoint the IFSC custodian, regulated interim custody permitted.
cards.means: Three moving parts of one design: a protective gate while schemes are small, a clean exit when raises fail, and a realistic runway for onshoring custody.
cards.trip: Each of these starts a CLOCK or sets a GATE — amendment mastery means knowing the dates, not just the rules.

questions.title: Episode 1: The Expired Extension
questions.question: What's wrong here?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — the extension is valid, since a one-time six-month extension at a 50% fee remains available
Only the fee is wrong — it should have been 25% of the fresh-scheme filing fee for a first extension
The application is fatally late — it had to be filed while the PPM was still valid — and the fee and the CO's position are outdated
The scheme should simply have declared its first close at the USD 1.8 Million it had already raised

questions.explanation:
The IFSCA (Fund Management) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026 (w.e.f. 30.01.2026) replaced the one-time extension with a multi-extension regime for restricted schemes: each extension is 6 months from expiry of existing validity, the application must be filed while the PPM is still valid, and fees are 25% (first) / 50% (each subsequent) of the prevailing fresh-scheme filing fee.
1. Fatal timing lapse: The PPM validity (12 months from taken-on-record) expired on 14 February 2026. Post-amendment Reg. 35(2) requires the extension application to be filed at such time when the placement memorandum is still valid. Filed 25 February 2026 = dead on arrival.
2. Wrong fee: Under the 2026 Amendment, the first extension attracts 25% of the applicable fresh-scheme filing fee; 50% applies only to each subsequent extension. The CO applied the pre-amendment rate.
3. Outdated legal position: "One-time 6-month extension" was the pre-30.01.2026 regime. The amendment permits multiple extensions of 6 months each — but only via applications filed during validity. The CO's file note is itself evidence of stale knowledge.

questions.title: Old Law or Current Law? — KMP Experience
questions.question:
An individual with post-qualification experience of at least 2 (two) years in an eligible institution in IFSC, India or any foreign jurisdiction and who holds valid certification(s), as specified by the Authority, shall be considered eligible for the KMP referred under sub-regulation (2).

Is this the current legal position or the pre-amendment position?

options.text: 2022 Framework (Old)
2025/2026 Framework (New)

questions.explanation: Current law. The 2026 Amendment substituted clause (b) of the KMP experience requirement and introduced graded routes: 5 years' experience in an "eligible institution" (a newly defined term), reduced to 3 years where the KMP holds a professional qualification, and a 2-year post-qualification route where the individual holds Authority-specified certifications. The pre-amendment text simply required 5 years in related securities-market activities.

questions.title: Old Law or Current Law? — Custodian in IFSC
questions.question:
In case of schemes which are required to appoint a custodian in IFSC, if any agreement has been entered into with a custodian which is not based in IFSC as on the date of notification of these regulations, such schemes shall be required to transition to an IFSC-based custodian.

Is this the current legal position or the pre-amendment position?

options.text: 2022 Framework (Old)
2025/2026 Framework (New)

questions.explanation: Pre-amendment. questions.title: Third-Party FM — Liability
questions.question: In a third-party fund management arrangement, if the third-party indemnifies the FME fully, the FME's regulatory liability for the schemes:

options.text: Transfers to the third-party manager to the full extent of the indemnity given
Is shared proportionately between them in the manner set out in the arrangement
Ceases once the Authority has approved the third-party arrangement in writing
Continues in full — the FME remains liable notwithstanding any indemnification arrangement

questions.explanation: Reg. 107C(4) is explicit: notwithstanding any arrangement with the third-party, including indemnification, the FME continues to be liable for all obligations arising from the arrangement. Indemnities are a commercial recovery mechanism inter se — they never dilute regulatory accountability. The FME must also strengthen compliance resources commensurate to scale (Reg. 107C(2)).

cards.title: “Approved” is not “notified”
cards.law: At its 29th meeting on 24 July 2026, the Authority approved a set of amendments to the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025 aimed at ease of doing business, greater disclosure and regulatory clarity.
cards.means: Approval is the decision to amend. The binding text arrives only when the amendment is notified in the Gazette. Until then, the 2025 Regulations as amended to 30 January 2026 remain the operative law — every drill in Modules 1–12 still states the law that binds you today.
cards.trip: Two opposite errors are possible. Acting on an unnotified change is a breach. Ignoring it in your planning is poor advice. A compliance officer tracks both columns.
cards.hook: Approval sets direction. Notification sets obligation.

cards.title: The contribution ceiling moves 10% → 25%
cards.law: In place of the existing 10% limit, FMEs and their associates having Indian ultimate beneficial owners will be permitted to contribute up to 25% of the corpus of VC Schemes and Restricted Schemes, where such schemes invest only in IFSC or foreign jurisdictions.
cards.means: Headroom for Indian-owned managers building an overseas track record. The floors (2.5% / 5% / USD 750K / USD 1.5M) are untouched — this raises the ceiling only, and only for a defined set.
cards.trip: It is conditional, not general: Indian UBO AND the scheme invests only in IFSC/foreign jurisdictions. Do not confuse it with the ceiling carve-out ALREADY in force under Reg. 28(1)/40 for FMEs resident outside India with no Indian UBO and not more than one-third of corpus in one investee.
cards.link: Modules 3 and 4 teach the binding 10% ceiling — that is still the examinable and enforceable figure.

cards.title: Timelines and valuation relax
cards.law: The scheme Annual Report timeline extends from four (4) to six (6) months from financial year end. Close-ended Restricted Schemes may move NAV computation and disclosure from semi-annual to annual, subject to prior approval of at least 75% of investors by value. Independent valuation is relaxed for investments in underlying scheme(s) already valued by an independent entity.
cards.means: Three operational easements. Note the middle one is not automatic — it is unlocked by an investor supermajority, the framework's recurring 75%-by-value lever.
cards.trip: Until notified, Reg. 134's four-month clock governs. Diarise four months; plan for six.
cards.link: Module 9 drills the binding four-month clock.

cards.title: New structures: blended finance
cards.law: VC Schemes and Restricted Schemes will be permitted to issue multiple classes of units with differential distribution rights — junior / subordinate classes may carry returns lower than, or bear losses higher than, their entitlement. Minimum investment in junior classes: USD 1 Million from non-individual Accredited Investors, or USD 2 Million from other investors. An ESG Scheme may accept funds as grants, subject to conditions.
cards.means: An enabling provision for blended finance — concessional or first-loss capital sitting beneath commercial capital to mobilise private money into climate and development projects.
cards.trip: The PPM must adequately and prominently disclose the classes, their distribution rights and the resulting risks; the FME and its KMPs must diligence compliance with Indian law and other Indian regulators.
cards.prov: Approved 24.07.2026 — Regulatory Framework for differential distribution
cards.hook: Junior units: USD 1Mn accredited (non-individual), USD 2Mn others.

cards.title: Investor protection tightens in parallel
cards.law: Retail offer-document disclosures expand to cover NAV computation methodology and conflicts of interest. Internal policies required under the regulations must be approved by the FME's governing body (or its delegate). Temporary deployment of monies before a scheme reaches minimum corpus will be permitted only in capital-preservation and liquidity instruments, with prior PPM/offer-document disclosure. The definition of “associate” expands to reach natural persons and non-body-corporate juridical persons holding a direct economic interest.
cards.means: Ease of business is paired with sharper governance. The wider “associate” definition matters most — it widens every conflict test that keys off that term.
cards.trip: A broader “associate” means transactions that pass your conflict screen today may need 75%-by-value investor approval once notified. Re-run the screen when it lands.

cards.title: Also approved — beyond the FM Regulations
cards.law: The Authority also approved an amendment to the IFSCA (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 on withdrawal of credit ratings by CRAs; the IFSCA (Prohibition of Market Abuse in Securities Markets) Regulations, 2026; and the IFSCA (Electronic Trading Platform) Regulations, 2026.
cards.means: The market-abuse framework is the one to watch from a fund seat: a unified regime prohibiting insider trading and fraudulent, manipulative and unfair trade practices across the IFSC securities market.
cards.trip: It is a separate regulation, not an FM Regulations amendment — but it will bind your dealing desk and your personal-trading policy all the same.
